Discover Japan's most effective walking method for seniors over 70 — a clinically studied technique called Interval Walking, developed by researchers at Shinshu University after a decade of research. Unlike conventional walking programs, this approach strategically alternates between slow and brisk pacing to reduce joint pressure, strengthen the muscles surrounding your knees, and improve overall stability — all without any equipment. In this video, I walk you through five knee-friendly exercises you can do right at home, designed specifically for older adults who want to stay active, independent, and pain-free. Your knees deserve better. Start today.

subtitles.plaintext:
What if I told you that Japan, the
country with more people living past 90
than anywhere else on Earth, has a
walking secret that has been quietly
protecting the knees of their seniors
for decades? And it is not a pill, not a
surgery, not an expensive piece of
equipment. It is simply the way they
walk.
One specific deliberate method that
takes the pressure off your joints with
every single step. And you can start
doing it today, right inside your own
home, in your living room, your hallway,
anywhere you have a few feet of clear
space.
Here is what makes this so important.
Most seniors over 70 are walking in a
way that slowly grinds down the
cartilage in their knees without ever
realizing it.
The damage builds quietly, step-by-step,
day-by-day, until one morning you wake
up and your knees simply will not
cooperate the way they used to.
But the Japanese figured out how to stop
this from happening. And today I am
going to show you exactly how.
We are going to cover the science behind
why this method works, five powerful
knee-friendly walking exercises based on
this Japanese method, all doable at
home, no equipment required, and then a
simple daily routine you can follow
starting tonight.
Before we dive in, if you haven't
subscribed yet, I recommend you hit that
button and turn on the bell, so you
never miss another health tip made just
for you. If you enjoyed this video, type
one in the comments. If not, type zero
to let me know how I can make better
content for you.
How it works.
So, what exactly is the Japanese walking
method? And why does it work so well for
seniors with sensitive or painful knees?
The method is called interval walking,
and it was developed by researchers at
Shinshu University in Japan after more
than 10 years of clinical study,
the core idea is simple. Instead of
walking at one steady pace the entire
time, you alternate between 3 minutes of
slow, controlled walking and 3 minutes
of slightly faster, more purposeful
walking, and you repeat that cycle
throughout your session.
Here is why this matters so much for
your knees. When you walk at the same
speed continuously, the same parts of
your cartilage absorb pressure with
every step. Over time, that repeated
stress causes breakdown. But when you
alternate your pace, the pressure shifts
and distributes more evenly across the
joint. Your knee gets a chance to
recover between intervals.
Blood flow increases. The muscles
surrounding the joint strengthen, and
the cartilage stays healthier longer.
That is the mechanism. That is why it
works.
Exercise one, the heel-first awareness
walk.
Why it matters.
This is the foundation of everything,
and it is the single most important
correction most seniors over 70 need to
make right now. After years of cautious,
shuffling steps, the natural heel strike
pattern that your body was designed to
use has quietly disappeared.
And when that happens, the pressure of
each step lands directly on the front of
your knee joint instead of being
absorbed and distributed properly
through the entire foot and leg.
The Japanese interval walking method
begins with one non-negotiable rule.
Every single step starts with the heel,
not the toe, not the flat of the foot,
the heel. This one change alone begins
redistributing the mechanical load away
from the most vulnerable parts of your
knee and toward the stronger muscles and
bones that are designed to handle it.
What makes this exercise different from
just walking is the speed.
You are going to slow everything down
dramatically, far slower than you think
is necessary, because at this pace your
brain can actually feel and correct each
step in real time. You are not just
walking, you are reprogramming a
movement pattern that has drifted off
course over many years. And that
reprogramming happens fastest when you
give your nervous system the time and
attention it needs to do the work
properly.
How to do it?
Find a clear hallway or open space along
a wall. Stand at one end with one hand
lightly touching the wall if you need
support. Begin walking at the slowest
pace you can physically manage. With
every single step, consciously reach
your heel slightly forward and let it
make contact with the ground first. Feel
the weight roll from your heel through
the arch across the ball of your foot
and push off gently through your toes.
Take 10 slow, deliberate steps forward,
turn carefully using small marching
steps, and walk back. That is one set.
Complete three sets, resting 30 seconds
between each one.
What to focus on?
Do not look down at your feet. Keep your
gaze forward, your chin level, your
shoulders relaxed. In real life, your
balance system needs to work while your
eyes are focused ahead, not at the
floor. This exercise begins training
that real-world skill from the very
first step. If you feel unsteady at any
point, slow down further and keep your
hand on the wall. There is no prize for
speed here.
Progress tip.
Once heel first contact feels natural
and automatic on flat ground, try the
same walk on a slightly different
surface, from hardwood to carpet, for
example. The subtle variation forces
your nervous system to adapt, which is
exactly the kind of challenge that
accelerates improvement in real-world
conditions.
If you're still watching and finding
these insights helpful, please comment
number one below to let me know you're
with me.
Now, let's move on to point number two.
Exercise two, the Japanese interval
walk.
Why it matters.
This is the heart of the entire method,
the core protocol that Japanese
researchers tested over 10 years and
found to be significantly more effective
than regular steady pace walking for
improving leg strength, cardiovascular
health, and joint comfort in adults over
65
The alternating slow-fast-slow rhythm is
not random. It is specifically designed
to build the muscles surrounding the
knee during the fast intervals and then
allow the joint to recover and replenish
its lubricating fluid during the slow
intervals. Done consistently, this cycle
strengthens the very muscles that
protect your knee from impact with every
step.
Most seniors who try this for the first
time are surprised by two things. First,
how manageable it feels because the slow
intervals give you genuine recovery time
built right into the workout. Second,
how much they feel it working because
those fast intervals, even though they
are not intense by any objective
standard, are asking muscles that have
been underused for months or years to
suddenly fire again.
That sensation is not discomfort. That
is progress.
How to do it.
Begin walking at a very easy, relaxed
pace, about 40 to 50% of your maximum
effort. You should be able to carry on a
full conversation without any
breathlessness. Maintain this slow pace
for exactly 3 minutes. Then, without
stopping, increase your pace to
approximately 70% effort, faster than
your comfortable pace, but not rushing
or straining.
Take slightly shorter steps, but move
them quicker. Maintain this faster pace
for 3 minutes, then return to slow.
Repeat this slow-fast cycle two full
times through for a total of 12 minutes
of interval walking. End with 2 minutes
of your slowest, most relaxed walking as
a cool down.
What to focus on?
During the fast intervals, keep your
posture upright. Do not lean forward as
your speed increases. This shifts load
onto the front of your knee and defeats
the purpose. Think tall spine, relaxed
shoulders, eyes forward. During the slow
intervals, use the time to consciously
check your heel strike from exercise
one. Slow is when you practice the
technique. Fast is when you build the
strength.
Progress tip.
Start with one complete slow fast cycle
if two feels like too much. Add the
second cycle only when the first feels
genuinely comfortable, not effortful.
Most people reach two full cycles within
1 to 2 weeks of consistent practice.
Exercise three, the high knee march.
Why it matters.
One of the most direct consequences of
the shuffle gait that develops in many
seniors over 70 is that the hip flexors,
the muscles responsible for lifting your
leg with each step, become progressively
weaker. And when these muscles weaken,
your foot clearance drops dangerously
close to the ground.
Every rug, every threshold, every slight
unevenness in the sidewalk becomes a
potential trip. But there is something
even more important happening underneath
all of this. Weak hip flexors force the
knee to compensate. The joint absorbs
more rotational stress than it was
designed to handle, and over time that
compensation is exactly what drives the
kind of knee pain that sneaks up on
seniors and seems to appear out of
nowhere.
This exercise directly rebuilds the hip
flexors and restores the lifting reflex
that keeps your feet safely off the
ground with every stride. While
simultaneously taking pressure off the
knee by strengthening the muscles above
it.
How to do it.
Stand behind a sturdy chair with both
hands resting lightly on the back for
support. Stand tall, back straight, chin
level, shoulders relaxed. Slowly lift
your right knee towards your chest as
high as you comfortably can without
leaning your upper body backward. Hold
for two full seconds at the top, then
lower your foot back to the floor slowly
and with complete control. Repeat on the
left side. That is one full repetition.
Complete 15 repetitions on each side, 30
total lifts, at a slow deliberate pace
throughout. The lift should feel
genuinely effortful. If it feels too
easy, you are not lifting high enough.
What to focus on?
The lowering phase is just as important
as the lifting phase. Do not let your
foot drop. Control the descent all the
way to the floor. This eccentric muscle
control is what stabilizes your knee
when your foot returns to the ground in
real walking, and it is one of the most
undertrained qualities in seniors over
70. Keep your standing leg very slightly
bent throughout. A locked knee during
this exercise places unnecessary stress
on the joint.
Progress tip.
As this becomes easier over one to two
weeks, practice the march while moving
slowly forward through your hallway.
Lifting each knee deliberately before
stepping, then placing your heel down
first. You are now combining this
exercise directly with exercise one,
creating the closest possible simulation
of proper walking mechanics that you can
train at home.
If you're still watching and finding
these insights valuable, please comment
number one below to let me know you're
here. Now, let's keep going with point
number four.
Exercise four, the slow-motion knee-safe
walk. Why it matters. Speed is where
proper walking mechanics break down.
When we walk at our normal everyday
pace, we rely almost entirely on habit
and momentum rather than conscious
muscle control. For a senior who is
rebuilding a walking pattern or trying
to protect vulnerable knee joints, that
reliance on habit is dangerous because
the habit itself may be the problem. The
slow-motion walk strips speed completely
out of the equation, forcing every
single muscle involved in walking to
work independently, deliberately, and
with full control. It is one of the most
powerful neurological training tools
available for relearning safe movement,
and it is one of the most direct ways to
reduce the impact forces that reach your
knee with every step.
Japanese physical therapists use
slow-motion walking drills extensively
in knee rehabilitation programs because
when you slow the movement down far
enough, patients can feel exactly where
their mechanics are breaking down and
correct them in real time.
That same principle applies perfectly
here.
How to do it.
Stand at one end of your hallway. Begin
walking at the absolute slowest pace you
can physically manage. So slow that each
complete step takes three to four full
seconds from lift-off to landing. Lift
your foot, pause briefly in the air,
reach the heel forward, lower it to the
floor with complete control, feel your
weight shift smoothly through the entire
foot, push off gently through the toes,
and begin the next step. Walk the full
length of the hallway in this
slow-motion style. Turn carefully at the
end using small controlled steps and
return. That is one set. Complete two
full sets with a 30-second rest between
them.
What to focus on.
This will feel strange, genuinely
strange. Slow-motion walking is
difficult precisely because it removes
all the shortcuts that habitual movement
depends on. Every wobble you feel is
your balance system being challenged and
strengthened. Every micro correction
your ankle makes is your nervous system
rebuilding its responsiveness.
Do not fight the wobble, work with it.
Stay near the wall, but try to use it as
a safety net rather than a crutch. The
goal is to feel the challenge and let
your body respond to it.
Progress tip.
Once you feel steady with eyes open, try
closing your eyes for just two or three
slow-motion steps while standing very
close to the wall. This dramatically
increases the proprioceptive demand and
accelerates the neurological adaptation
you are building.
Open your eyes immediately if you feel
any loss of stability.
Exercise five.
Sideways walking.
Why it matters.
Here is something most people never
think about when it comes to walking
safely after 70.
Almost every exercise you have ever been
shown, every balance drill, every
strength routine, every walking program,
trains your body to move in one
direction only.
Forward. And while forward movement is
obviously important, the reality of
everyday life is far more demanding than
a straight line down a hallway.
Think about the moments in your day when
you actually move sideways, sliding
along a row of seats at church, stepping
to the side to let someone pass you on a
narrow sidewalk, reaching across your
body to grab something from a shelf,
shifting your weight sideways to step
out of the bathtub. Every one of these
movements requires your hips, knees, and
ankles to work in a direction they
almost never get trained. And when those
muscles are weak in that lateral
direction, even a simple sideways shift
of your weight can send you off balance
in an instant.
Japanese physical therapists have used
sideways walking as a a rehabilitation
tool for decades, specifically because
it activates the hip abductors, the
muscles along the outside of your hips
and thighs, in a way that no amount of
forward walking ever can.
These muscles are the unsung heroes of
knee stability. When they are strong,
they keep your knee properly aligned
with every step. When they are weak, the
knee drifts inward, the joint absorbs
uneven pressure, and both your stability
and your comfort suffer significantly.
The good news is that sideways walking
is one of the gentlest, most
knee-friendly movements you can do
because it involves almost no impact, no
twisting, and no sudden changes in
direction.
It is smooth, controlled, and safe even
for seniors with sensitive joints.
How to do it.
Stand sideways along a clear wall with
one hand lightly touching it for
support. Place your feet hip-width
apart, toes pointing forward, knees very
slightly bent, never locked straight.
Now, take a slow, controlled step to the
right with your right foot, about
shoulder-width out. Then, bring your
left foot to meet it, returning to your
starting hip-width stance. That is one
step. Continue stepping in the same
direction for 10 full steps, then
reverse, leading with your left foot,
and take 10 steps back to where you
started. That is one complete set. Rest
for 30 seconds and repeat two more times
for a total of three sets in each
direction. What to focus on.
Keep your toes pointing forward
throughout. Do not let them rotate
outward as you step. Keep your knees
soft and slightly bent the entire time.
Stand tall with your shoulders relaxed
and your gaze forward, not down at your
feet. The movement should feel smooth
and deliberate, like you're sliding
along a track rather than hopping from
side to side. If you hear your feet
shuffling or scraping the floor, slow
down and lift each foot more consciously
with every step.
Progress tip.
Once three sets feel comfortable and
controlled, try the same exercise
without touching the wall. Arms extended
slightly out to your sides for balance
instead. This dramatically increases the
demand on your hip stabilizers and your
ankle balance system simultaneously.
You can also add a light resistance band
just above your knees for even greater
hip abductor activation, but only after
the body weight version feels genuinely
solid and easy.
Your daily routine.
Here is how to build this into your
daily life in a way that is realistic,
sustainable, and genuinely effective.
Every morning before you do anything
else, do 5 minutes of slow walking
inside your home. Down the hallway,
around the living room, it does not
matter where. This wakes up the fluid in
your knee joints and gets blood moving
before your body has to bear full weight
on cold, stiff cartilage.
Think of it as lubricating the hinges
before you open the door.
Then, once during the afternoon, after
lunch works beautifully, do your full
15-minute Japanese interval walking
session using the five exercises I am
about to show you.
Finally, in the evening, 2 minutes of
slow walking before bed helps flush the
inflammation that naturally builds up in
the joints throughout the day. Morning,
afternoon, evening. That is it. Three
small commitments, and over time the
difference in how your knees feel will
genuinely surprise you.
Important safety warning. Before we get
into the exercises, please take this
seriously because your safety comes
first, always.
If you have had a recent knee
replacement, are being treated for
severe osteoarthritis, or have been told
by your doctor to avoid weight-bearing
activity, please speak with your
physician before attempting any of these
movements.
Always practice near a wall, chair, or
countertop you can reach instantly. Wear
non-slip shoes or go barefoot on a safe
surface. Never socks on hardwood. If you
feel sharp pain, sudden dizziness, or
anything that does not feel right, stop
immediately. No exercise here is worth
risking your safety. Move at your own
pace. Your body will tell you when it is
ready for more.
If you enjoyed this video, please leave
a comment with one. If not, feel free to
comment with zero. Your feedback means a
lot to us. Don't forget to like, share,
and subscribe to our YouTube channel for
more content like this.
Thank you for watching and here's to
living life on your own terms.

text:
If you've been drifting sideways when you walk or grabbing walls just to feel steady, your legs are not the problem. As a physician, I see this pattern constantly in patients over 70 — and the real cause is reduced blood flow to the cerebellum, the brain's balance command center. The vertebral arteries that feed this critical region travel directly through your cervical spine, meaning chronic neck tension can quietly compress them over time. In this video, I'll show you 8 targeted exercises — 3 neck release movements and 5 cerebellum training drills — that address the root cause and help restore steady, confident walking. No equipment needed. Just 12 minutes a day.

subtitles.plaintext:
What if I told you that the reason you
drift when you walk, that quiet pull to
one side, that moment of hesitation
before your body decides which way is
straight, has nothing to do with your
legs at all? And what if I told you that
the real cause is something happening
inside your neck right now that nobody
has ever explained to you?
Because here's what I see happen over
and over again. Someone starts drifting
when they walk. They reach for walls
when they stand up. Their body hesitates
in ways it never used to. They go to
their doctor and they hear the same
things every time.
Watch your step. Hold the railing. Maybe
it's just age.
So they go home, try a few leg
exercises, and nothing changes. The
drifting continues. The hesitation
continues. And eventually they accept it
as inevitable.
I am here today to tell you it is not
inevitable. I am going to explain
exactly what is happening inside your
body in plain, simple terms. And then
I'm going to walk you through eight
exercises that target the real problem
directly. No gym, no equipment, just a
wall, a chair, and less than 12 minutes
a day.
Before we dive in, if you haven't
subscribed yet, I recommend you hit that
button and turn on the bell so you never
miss another health tip made just for
you. If you enjoy this video, type one
in the comments. If not, type zero to
let me know how I can make better
content for you.
What's actually happening in your body?
Here is the truth that most people never
hear.
When you start drifting when you walk,
the problem is almost never your legs.
At the base of your skull sits a
structure called the cerebellum, your
brain's balance command center. Every
second you are upright, it receives
signals from your muscles, your joints,
your inner ear, and your eyes, and uses
all of that to make constant tiny
corrections that keep you walking
straight.
When it's working well, you never feel
it. You just walk. When it starts
running at reduced capacity, you drift,
you grab walls, and every step feels
slightly uncertain.
Now, here is the part that changes
everything.
The arteries that carry blood to your
cerebellum travel through the bones of
your neck, one vertebra at a time.
So, when those neck muscles become
chronically tight from years of posture
habits or old injuries, they quietly
compress those arteries and reduce the
blood supply reaching your cerebellum.
Not dramatically, but enough over months
and years to slowly erode your balance
and coordination.
That is the real mechanism. And fixing
it means addressing both sides,
releasing the restriction in your neck,
and retraining the cerebellum directly.
That is exactly what these eight
exercises do.
>> The exercises.
We work in two groups today. Group one
releases the neck tension, group two
trains your cerebellum. You need both.
They work together.
Group one.
Neck release exercises.
Exercise one.
Base of neck rotation release.
Why this matters. The junction where
your neck meets your upper back is one
of the two areas most likely to
accumulate stiffness that compresses the
arteries feeding your cerebellum.
This movement gently mobilizes that
exact zone.
How to do it. Sit in a sturdy chair with
your back straight. Gently drop your
chin slightly toward your chest. Place
two fingertips against the bony bump at
the very base of your neck, that
prominent vertebra where the neck meets
the upper back.
Slowly rotate your head to the right
using your fingertips to apply gentle
guiding pressure in the same direction.
Move only as far as comfortable. You
want a mild stretching sensation, never
pain. Hold at that gentle end point for
3 to 4 seconds. Slowly return to center.
Repeat on the left side.
Do five repetitions on each side.
Practice once in the morning and once in
the evening. Most people notice their
range of motion gradually increasing
over the first 1 to 2 weeks as the
stiffness begins to ease.
Exercise two, side neck stretch.
Why this matters. The large diagonal
muscle running from behind your ear down
to your collarbone is one of the most
chronically overworked muscles in the
body. When it stays tight, it places
sustained pressure on the structures
running through your cervical spine,
including the arteries feeding your
cerebellum.
How to do it. Place one hand flat
against your collarbone on one side and
press gently downward to anchor the
tissue. Slowly tilt your head toward the
opposite shoulder and lift your chin
very slightly upward. You should feel a
clear, deep stretch running along the
full side of your neck.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds, breathing
slowly and steadily. Do not pull or
force. Let gravity and time do the work.
Return slowly to center and repeat on
the other side.
Do two repetitions on each side per
session.
Exercise three, neck self massage.
Why this matters. Stretching releases
muscle length. Massage releases the
deeper tissue tension that builds up
over years and doesn't respond to
stretching alone. The kind that quietly
narrows the space around those cervical
arteries.
How to do it. Using the fingertips of
both hands, begin at the base of your
skull and apply firm circular pressure
as you work slowly down both sides of
your neck toward the base.
Spend about 60 to 90 seconds on each
side.
Look for areas that feel noticeably
tighter or more tender than the
surrounding tissue. Spend a little extra
time on those spots, not digging in
painfully, but applying steady, gentle
pressure until you feel the tissue begin
to soften.
Do this once daily, ideally in the
morning before or after the other two
neck exercises.
>> Group two, cerebellum training
exercises.
Exercise four, slow-motion straight-line
walk.
Why this matters? Before you can retrain
your walking pattern, you need to slow
it down enough that your brain can
consciously register and correct each
step. Slow-motion walking strips away
the momentum that normally covers up
your weaknesses and forces every muscle
and every balance signal to work with
full intention.
How to do it? Find a clear hallway.
Place one hand lightly on the wall if
you need support to start. Begin walking
at the slowest pace you can manage. So
slow that each step takes a full 3 to 4
seconds to complete. Lift your foot
deliberately, pause briefly in the air,
reach your heel slightly forward and
lower it to the floor with full control.
Feel your weight shift through your foot
before taking the next step.
Walk 10 steps forward. Turn carefully
using small marching steps. Walk 10
steps back. That is one set.
Complete three sets.
What to focus on? Look straight ahead,
not down at your feet. Your balance
system needs to work while your eyes are
focused on where you are going, not
where your feet are landing.
The wobbling you feel during this
exercise is your cerebellum actively
working. That is not a problem. That is
the entire point.
Progress tip. Once this feels smooth,
try it on carpet versus hardwood. The
slight surface change forces your
nervous system to adapt and generalize
the pattern, which is what you need for
real-world safety.
Exercise five, tandem heel-to-toe walk.
Why this matters? This directly
simulates the kind of walking that
causes the most falls. Narrow hallways,
stepping carefully around furniture,
navigating tight spaces. It trains
dynamic balance, which is your balance
while you are actually in motion, not
standing still.
How to do it? Stand at one end of a
clear hallway with one hand lightly
touching the wall. Place your right foot
directly in front of your left so that
the heel of your right foot nearly
touches the toes of your left. Then step
your left foot forward in the same way,
heel-to-toe in a perfectly straight
line.
Take 10 steps forward.
Turn carefully.
Take 10 steps back. That is one set.
Complete two sets.
What to focus on? Keep your eyes
forward, not down at your feet. Walk
slowly and with full control. If you
need to touch the wall for a moment,
that is completely fine. Touch it and
continue. Consistency matters far more
than perfection here.
Progress tip. As this becomes easier,
try it with your arms crossed over your
chest instead of extended for balance.
This removes the arm compensation and
forces your core and ankles to take on
more of the stabilizing work.
Exercise six, standing marches with
cross body
tap.
Why this matters? This rebuilds two
things at once, the hip flexor strength
needed to lift your feet clearly off the
ground with each step, and the cross
body coordination that is one of the
cerebellum's most important jobs. Cross
body movement activates the neural
pathways between the two hemispheres of
the brain, which is essential for
smooth, coordinated walking.
How to do it? Stand tall behind a sturdy
chair with both hands lightly resting on
the back. Lift your right knee towards
your chest as high as you comfortably
can. As your knee rises, tap it with
your left hand. Lower the right leg with
control, then lift your left knee and
tap it with your right hand. That is one
repetition.
Do 10 repetitions on each side, 20
total. Move slowly and deliberately. The
tapping hand and the rising knee should
meet at exactly the same moment. That
precise timing is what trains the
cerebellum.
Progress tip. Once this feels
comfortable, try it without holding the
chair. Arms extended to your sides
instead. Eventually, try two or three
reps with your eyes closed to deepen the
neurological challenge.
Exercise seven, fixed point turn.
Why this matters? Dizziness and
disorientation during turning movements.
Pivoting in the kitchen, turning to look
behind you, getting up and changing
direction, is one of the most common
triggers for falls after 70.
This exercise trains exactly that skill
by forcing your visual system and your
vestibular system to coordinate during
rotation, which is precisely the job the
cerebellum struggles with when its blood
supply is compromised.
How to do it? Stand facing a wall with a
sturdy chair or counter top nearby.
Choose a fixed point at roughly eye
level. A light switch, a picture frame,
any clear mark on the Lock your gaze on
that point.
Now take three slow steps and execute a
complete 360° turn. During the turn,
keep your eyes locked on that fixed
point for as long as physically
possible. The moment the turn is
complete, find that same point again
immediately.
Do five full turns per session. Start
very slowly. As this becomes easier over
the following weeks, gradually increase
the speed of the turn.
What to focus on?
Do not close your eyes during this one.
The entire benefit comes from the active
coordination between what your eye see
and what your inner ear feels during the
rotation. Stay near the wall, especially
in the first week.
Exercise eight, multi-direction weight
shifts.
Why this matters? Most falls do not
happen going straight forward. They
happen when you reach sideways, turn
slightly, or shift your weight in an
unexpected direction. This exercise
trains your ability to move your center
of gravity in multiple directions and
recover back to center, which is the
core skill your body needs to catch
itself before a stumble becomes a fall.
How to do it? Stand behind a sturdy
chair with both hands resting lightly on
the back. Feet hip-width apart, back
straight.
Slowly shift your weight to your right
foot, lifting your left foot just 1 in
off the floor.
Hold for 3 seconds. Return to center.
Now shift to your left foot, lifting the
right foot just 1 in. Hold for 3
seconds. Return to center.
Now shift your weight gently forward
onto the balls of your feet, just far
enough to feel the challenge without
your heels leaving the floor.
Hold 3 seconds. Return.
Then shift gently backward onto your
heels. Hold 3 seconds. Return.
That full sequence, right, left,
forward, back, is one complete round. Do
three rounds.
Progress.
Tip. As you get stronger, gradually
reduce your grip on the chair, from full
hands to fingertips only to no support
at all. Each step down forces your
ankles, hips, and core to take on more
of the stabilizing work.
Important safety note.
Now that you have seen all eight
exercises, I want to stop for a moment
before you begin
because your safety is the most
important thing here, and I would never
forgive myself if someone got hurt
trying to follow along.
First, please understand that these
exercises are designed for general use
by healthy older adults. If you have
been diagnosed with a neurological
condition such as Parkinson's disease,
have a history of stroke, or have been
told by a doctor that you have
significant vertebral artery disease, or
severe cervical instability, please
speak with your physician or a licensed
physical therapist before attempting any
of these movements. Your situation may
require a modified or closely supervised
approach, and that is completely okay.
Second, for the neck release exercises
specifically, never force any movement.
The stretches and rotations in group one
should always feel like a gentle, mild
pull. Never sharp, never pinching, and
never accompanied by dizziness or a
tingling sensation down your arms.
If you feel any of those things, stop
immediately and consult your doctor
before continuing. The neck is a
sensitive area, and patience here will
serve you far better than pushing too
hard, too fast.
Third, for the balance and walking
exercises in group two, always have
something within reach before you start.
A wall, a sturdy chair, a countertop, it
does not matter which as long as it is
there. And this is not because I expect
you to fall, it is because having that
safety net nearby lets you train with
more confidence and less tension, which
actually makes every single exercise
more effective.
Fourth, never do these exercises in
socks on a hard floor. Socks on smooth
surfaces are one of the most common
causes of slips at home. Go barefoot if
you can. It is actually ideal for
balance training because it maximizes
the sensory feedback your brain receives
from the ground. If you prefer footwear,
choose shoes with a non-slip sole.
Fifth and most importantly, if at any
point during any of these exercises, you
experience sharp pain, sudden dizziness,
a feeling of the room spinning, or
anything that simply does not feel
right, stop immediately. Do not push
through it. There is no movement here
worth risking an injury over.
Work at your own pace, progress on your
own timeline, and let your body tell you
when it is ready for more.
That is how lasting change is built.
Your daily routine.
Here is the simplest way to fit all
eight exercises into your day.
Every morning, spend 5 minutes on the
three neck release exercises, the
rotation, the side stretch, and the
self-massage. Think of this as opening
the pathway so your cerebellum can
receive what it needs throughout the
day.
Then, at any point during the day, even
in short 2-minute bursts, work through
the five cerebellum training exercises.
The slow-motion walk and heel-to-toe
walk can be done in any hallway. The
marches, turns, and weight shifts can
all be done in a small space next to a
chair.
The entire routine takes less than 12
minutes total, and these work best done
consistently, a little every day, rather
than long sessions once or twice a week.
Do not skip the days when you feel
steady. Those are actually the most
important days of all. Every repetition
builds the neural pathway that fires
automatically the next time your balance
is challenged. You are doing the work
now so your body can protect you later,
in that split second when it matters
most.
Closing.
The drifting, the wobbling, the reaching
for walls, none of that has to be the
final chapter. Your cerebellum has not
given up. It may simply need better
input, better blood flow, and better
daily practice. When you give your brain
the right challenge consistently, it can
respond, slowly, quietly, and steadily.
Before you leave this video, remember
this. The people who improve the most
are not always the ones who push the
hardest. They are the ones who show up
every day even when nothing seems to be
changing because the brain often
improves before you can feel it. New
pathways are being trained, old signals
are being reawakened, and then one
morning you walk across the kitchen and
realize something important you did not
reach for the wall. You simply walked.
So, start small today. Do the neck
release. Try the slow-motion walk. That
is enough for day one. Then add one more
exercise every few days. Your goal is
not perfection. Your goal is to teach
your body one careful repetition at a
time how to trust the ground again. Give
yourself 6 weeks of steady practice and
you may begin to feel more control, more
confidence, and more trust in your own
steps again.
And please, do not keep this to
yourself. If you know someone who grabs
the counter when they stand, avoids
walking outside, or feels nervous
turning in the hallway, share this video
with them. This simple information may
help them feel safer, steadier, and more
independent.
One more thing before you go. Balance is
only one part of fall prevention. The
next piece is leg strength. Even when
your balance improves, your legs still
need the power to catch you in that
split second when it matters most. That
is why I made a dedicated video on safe
leg strengthening exercises for people
over 70. No gym, no equipment, and easy
to follow at home. That video is on the
screen right now. Click it next and I
will walk you through it step by step.
If you enjoyed this video, please leave
a comment with one. If not, feel free to
comment with zero. Your feedback means a
lot to us. Don't forget to like, share,
and subscribe to our YouTube channel for
more content like this.
Thank you for watching and here's to
living life on your own terms.

text:
After 70, many falls begin with something most people overlook: weak ankles. In this senior health video, Doctor Thomas explains how your ankles help control balance, foot clearance, and steady walking. You’ll learn a simple 3-minute ankle routine designed to wake up the small stabilizing muscles, improve foot awareness, and help you feel safer with everyday movement. These exercises are gentle, practical, and can be done at home with a sturdy chair for support. Always move slowly, stay safe, and speak with your doctor or physical therapist if you have pain, dizziness, neuropathy, or a recent ankle injury.

subtitles.plaintext:
What if I told you that something you do
dozens of times every single day,
something so automatic you never even

Soulevez votre pied droit de quelques
centimètres. En utilisant votre pied
comme un stylo et votre gros orteil
comme pointe, tracez lentement chaque
lettre de l'alphabet dans l'air. A, B,
C, et ainsi de suite. Faites chaque
lettre aussi grande que vous le pouvez
confortablement. Le mouvement doit
provenir entièrement de votre cheville
, pas de votre genou ou de votre hanche
. Faites l'alphabet complet avec le
pied droit. Puis passez au pied gauche.
Sur quoi se concentrer ? Bougez
lentement et avec intention. Plus
chaque lettre est grande et
délibérée, plus vous obtenez
d'activation musculaire. Si votre
cheville semble raide sur les
premières lettres, c'est tout à fait
normal. La raideur diminuera à mesure
que vous continuez. Conseil de
progression. Avec le temps, essayez de
faire cet exercice les yeux fermés.
Supprimer l'apport visuel force votre
système proprioceptif à travailler
davantage, accélérant ainsi
l'entraînement neurologique. Exercice
deux, la marche sur les talons.
Pourquoi est-ce important ? Le muscle
qui longe l'avant de votre jambe, le
jambier antérieur, est l'un des
muscles les plus négligés dans la
prévention des chutes. Chaque fois que
vous levez le pied pour faire un pas,
ce muscle contrôle la manière dont
votre pied se soulève et se pose.
Lorsqu'il est faible, votre pied a
tendance à traîner légèrement ou à
claquer au sol au lieu d'être posé de
manière contrôlée, ce qui est l'une
des causes principales de
trébuchements sur un sol inégal. La
marche sur les talons cible directement
ce muscle. Comment faire ? Tenez-vous
derrière une chaise stable avec vos
mains posées légèrement sur le
dossier pour le soutien. Soulevez vos
deux pointes de pieds du sol de sorte
à être en équilibre uniquement sur
vos talons. Dans cette position,
marchez lentement vers l'avant. 10
petits pas sur vos talons, en gardant
les orteils relevés tout du long. Puis
marchez 10 pas vers l'arrière. Cela
constitue une série. Faites deux
séries. Sur quoi se concentrer ?
Gardez vos pas petits et contrôlés.
Ne vous précipitez pas. Plus vous
bougez lentement, plus votre jambier
antérieur doit travailler dur.
Tenez-vous bien droit tout au long de
l'exercice. Ne vous penchez pas en
avant et ne laissez pas votre buste
compenser. Conseil de progression. À
mesure que cela devient plus facile,
essayez de lâcher la chaise pour que
seuls vos doigts la touchent. À terme,
essayez de le faire sans aucun support.
Bras tendus sur les côtés pour
l'équilibre. Exercice trois, cercles
de cheville sur une jambe. Pourquoi
est-ce important ? Se tenir sur une
jambe tout en bougeant l'autre est l'un
des exercices d'équilibre les plus
fonctionnels, car il reproduit
fidèlement ce que fait votre corps à
chaque pas. Pendant une fraction de
seconde à chaque enjambée, tout le
poids de votre corps repose sur un seul
pied. Cet exercice entraîne la
cheville de la jambe d'appui à rester
stable sous la charge, tout en
améliorant la mobilité du pied en
mouvement. Une combinaison puissante
pour la prévention des chutes. Comment
faire ? Tenez-vous près d'un mur ou
d'une chaise pour vous soutenir.
Transférez votre poids sur votre pied
droit, en gardant le genou droit
légèrement fléchi. Ne le verrouillez
jamais. Soulevez lentement votre pied
gauche de quelques centimètres. Faites
maintenant pivoter votre pied gauche en
décrivant de grands cercles lents. 10
cercles dans le sens des aiguilles
d'une montre, puis 10 dans le sens
inverse. Gardez votre cheville droite,
celle qui porte le poids, aussi
immobile et stable que possible.
Ensuite, changez de côté. Tenez-vous
sur votre pied gauche et faites tourner
le droit. Effectuez deux séries de
chaque côté. Sur quoi se concentrer ?
Le véritable entraînement se joue au
niveau de la cheville d'appui, pas du
pied qui bouge. Concentrez-vous sur la
stabilité de votre pied d'appui, la
répartition du poids et la souplesse
de votre genou. Respirez lentement et
régulièrement. Conseil de progression
. Une fois à l'aise, essayez d'enlever
un doigt du mur au lieu de toute la
main, puis deux doigts. L'objectif à
terme est de laisser votre main flotter
près du support plutôt que de le
saisir, en ne le touchant qu'en cas de
nécessité. Quatrième exercice : le
froissement de serviette. Pourquoi
est-ce important ? La voûte plantaire
et les muscles intrinsèques du pied
sont directement liés à la capacité
de stabilisation de la cheville.
Lorsque ces muscles sont faibles, ce
qui arrive après des années de
chaussures de soutien sur des surfaces
planes, le pied s'affaisse légèrement
vers l'intérieur, compromettant la
cheville. Le froissement de serviette
réactive ces muscles profonds
rapidement et efficacement,
rétablissant la base dont votre
cheville a besoin. Comment faire.
Asseyez-vous sur une chaise stable et
placez une petite serviette à plat sur
le sol devant vous. Posez vos deux
pieds nus sur la serviette. En
utilisant uniquement vos orteils et
sans décoller le talon du sol,
froissez la serviette vers vous pour
l'accumuler sous vos pieds. Écartez
ensuite largement vos orteils pour
relâcher et étaler à nouveau la
serviette. C'est une répétition.
Effectuez 15 répétitions.
Reposez-vous 30 secondes. Puis faites
une deuxième série de 15. Sur quoi se
concentrer ? Gardez vos talons au sol
à tout moment. Le mouvement doit
provenir exclusivement de vos orteils
et de votre voûte plantaire. Vous
ressentirez peut-être une légère
fatigue au niveau de la voûte
plantaire ou de la plante du pied.
C'est exactement le signe que les bons
muscles travaillent. Conseil de
progression. À mesure que cela devient
plus facile, essayez de le faire un
pied à la fois, ce qui augmente
considérablement la difficulté. Vous
pouvez également passer à une
serviette plus épaisse ou plus lourde
pour augmenter la résistance.
Cinquième exercice, la position en pas
décalé. Maintien. Pourquoi est-ce
important ? Ce dernier exercice est
celui qui rassemble tout. La position
en pas décalé, un pied légèrement
devant l'autre, est celle que votre
corps adopte pour une part importante
de chaque pas que vous faites. C'est
aussi l'une des positions les plus
instables pour quelqu'un ayant des
chevilles fragiles. En maintenant cette
position et en laissant votre cheville
effectuer les micro-corrections
continues nécessaires pour vous tenir
debout, vous entraînez directement la
réactivité en temps réel qui évite
qu'un faux pas ne devienne une chute.
Comment le faire ? Tenez-vous près
d'un mur ou d'une chaise par sécurité
. Placez votre pied droit environ un
demi-pas devant votre pied gauche. Pas
une foulée complète, juste un court
décalage. Les deux pieds doivent être
orientés vers l'avant. Votre poids
doit être réparti entre les deux
pieds. Maintenez cette position pendant
20 à 30 secondes, en vous efforçant
de rester aussi immobile que possible
tout en laissant vos chevilles faire
les petits ajustements nécessaires
pour garder l'équilibre. Ensuite,
inversez en plaçant le pied gauche
devant et maintenez à nouveau pendant
20 à 30 secondes. Effectuez deux
maintiens de chaque côté. Sur quoi se
concentrer ? Laissez le vacillement se
produire. Ces petits mouvements subtils
que vous ressentez dans votre cheville
ne sont pas le signe que vous échouez.
Ce sont exactement le stimulus
d'entraînement dont vous avez besoin.
Chaque micro-correction effectuée par
votre cheville est votre système
nerveux qui reconstruit sa réactivité
. Le but n'est pas d'être parfaitement
immobile. Le but est de rester debout
pendant que votre cheville fait son
travail. Conseil de progression :
fermez les yeux une fois que vous vous
sentez stable dans cette position. Vous
remarquerez immédiatement à quel
point vos chevilles doivent travailler
davantage sans repère visuel et à
quelle vitesse votre système
d'équilibre s'adapte au défi.
Avertissement de sécurité important.
Maintenant que vous comprenez les cinq
exercices, veuillez prendre un moment
pour écouter cet avertissement de
sécurité avant de commencer à les
pratiquer, car votre sécurité est la
seule chose qui compte ici.
Premièrement, si vous êtes
actuellement traité pour une blessure
à la cheville, une fracture, un
problème de tendon d'Achille ou toute
forme d'arthrite affectant vos
articulations du pied ou de la cheville
, veuillez consulter votre médecin ou
votre kinésithérapeute avant de
tenter ces mouvements. Certains de ces
exercices peuvent nécessiter d'être
modifiés ou évités complètement
selon votre condition spécifique.
Deuxièmement, si vous avez reçu un
diagnostic de neuropathie
périphérique, une affection qui
réduit la sensation dans vos pieds,
soyez très prudent et ayez toujours
une surface solide à portée de main.
Une sensibilité réduite signifie un
retour d'information réduit, ce qui
veut dire que les problèmes
d'équilibre peuvent vous surprendre
plus facilement. Troisièmement, faites
toujours ces exercices près d'un mur,
d'un comptoir ou d'une chaise robuste.
Non pas parce que vous vous attendez à
perdre l'équilibre, mais parce que
cette sécurité à proximité permet
à votre système nerveux de se
détendre, ce qui rend les exercices
plus efficaces. Quatrièmement, soyez
pieds nus si vous le pouvez. Pour
l'entraînement des chevilles et des
pieds en particulier, le contact direct
avec le sol augmente considérablement
le retour sensoriel que reçoit votre
cerveau. Et ce retour d'information est
tout l'intérêt de ce que nous faisons
ici. Si vous devez porter des
chaussures, choisissez une chaussure à
semelle fine et antidérapante. Ne
faites jamais ces exercices en
chaussettes sur un sol dur. Et enfin,
si un mouvement provoque une douleur
aiguë, des étourdissements importants
ou quoi que ce soit qui semble anormal,
arrêtez immédiatement. Aucun exercice
de cette routine ne justifie de forcer
malgré la douleur. Travaillez dans ce
qui semble sûr et confortable pour
votre corps, et progressez à votre
propre rythme. Conclusion. Après 26
ans de travail avec des patients de
plus de 70 ans, voici ce que je sais
être vrai. Les personnes qui
vieillissent le mieux ne sont pas
celles qui arrêtent de bouger par
prudence. Ce sont celles qui apprennent
à bouger plus intelligemment. Elles
comprennent que la sécurité ne
signifie pas rester immobile. La
sécurité signifie prêter attention
aux petits signaux que votre corps vous
envoie et adopter des habitudes simples
qui vous aident à rester stable,
indépendant et confiant. C'est
exactement ce dont il s'agissait
aujourd'hui. Pas un entraînement
difficile, pas un défi de fitness, pas
quelque chose qui nécessite une salle
de sport, un équipement spécial ou un
équilibre parfait pour commencer.
Aujourd'hui, il était question de vos
chevilles. L'une des parties du corps
les plus négligées en matière de
prévention des chutes. Chaque fois que
vous vous tenez debout, que vous vous
tournez, que vous attrapez quelque
chose, que vous traversez la cuisine,
que vous descendez un trottoir ou que
vous sortez du lit, vos chevilles
travaillent discrètement en
arrière-plan pour vous maintenir droit
. Et lorsque ces petits muscles et
capteurs autour de la cheville
deviennent faibles ou lents, votre
corps peut ne pas réagir assez vite
lorsque le sol change, lorsque votre
poids se déplace ou lorsque votre pied
se pose un peu différemment que prévu
. C'est là qu'un petit faux pas peut
devenir quelque chose de beaucoup plus
sérieux. Mais la bonne nouvelle est
celle-ci. La force et la réactivité
des chevilles peuvent s'améliorer.
J'ai vu des patients dans la
quatre-vingtaine et la
quatre-vingt-dixaine devenir plus
stables, plus confiants et moins
effrayés par les mouvements du
quotidien simplement en pratiquant de
petits exercices comme ceux que nous
avons vus aujourd'hui. Ils n'ont pas
changé leur vie grâce à un effort
spectaculaire. Ils l'ont changée avec
5 minutes de pratique régulière et
attentive. Le tracé de l'alphabet avec
la cheville aide celle-ci à bouger
dans plus de directions. La marche sur
les talons réveille le muscle à
l'avant de votre jambe qui aide à
lever le pied. Les cercles de cheville
sur une jambe entraînent la cheville
d'appui à stabiliser votre corps en
charge. Le mouvement de la serviette
avec les orteils renforce les petits
muscles de la voûte plantaire. Et la
posture en pas décalé apprend à vos
chevilles à faire ces minuscules
corrections en temps réel qui évitent
qu'un faux pas ne devienne une chute.
Donc si vous vous êtes senti un peu
raide, un peu instable ou surpris par
la concentration nécessaire, ne vous
découragez pas. Cela ne signifie pas
que vous avez échoué. Cela signifie
que vous avez identifié le système
qui a besoin d'attention. Ces petits
déséquilibres ne sont pas vos ennemis
. C'est votre système nerveux qui
s'exerce. Le but n'est pas d'être
parfait. Le but est de rester en
sécurité, d'être régulier et de
donner à votre corps une raison de
redevenir plus réactif. Commencez
doucement. Choisissez un ou deux
exercices si c'est tout ce que vous
pouvez faire aujourd'hui. Gardez une
chaise solide, un comptoir ou un mur à
portée de main. Bougez lentement.
Respirez normalement. Ne vous
précipitez jamais. Et si vous avez une
blessure à la cheville, de l'arthrite,
des problèmes au tendon d'Achille, une
neuropathie périphérique, des
étourdissements ou tout ce qui affecte
votre équilibre, veuillez consulter
votre médecin ou kinésithérapeute
avant de commencer. La prudence n'est
pas une faiblesse. La prudence est une
sagesse. Désormais, des chevilles plus
fortes vous protégeront dès la base.
Mais voici une réflexion que je veux
vous laisser avant de partir. Même
avec des chevilles plus fortes, la
manière dont beaucoup de personnes de
plus de 70 ans marchent peut encore
augmenter silencieusement leur risque
de chute. Il y a trois habitudes de
marche spécifiques que je vois sans
cesse dans mon cabinet. Des habitudes
si courantes que la plupart des gens
pensent qu'elles font partie du
vieillissement, mais elles ne sont pas
sans danger. L'une affecte la façon
dont votre pied se pose, l'autre votre
manière de tourner, et la troisième
votre équilibre avant même que vous
ne réalisiez votre instabilité. Dans
ma prochaine vidéo, je vais vous
montrer exactement quelles sont ces
trois habitudes et comment les corriger
sans équipement ni routine complexe,
juste avec des mouvements plus
intelligents, dès votre prochain pas.
Cette vidéo s'affiche sur votre écran
en ce moment. Cliquez dessus et je vous
y retrouve. Et avant de partir,
partagez cette vidéo avec quelqu'un
qui vous est cher, un conjoint, un ami,
un frère ou une sœur, un voisin, ou
toute personne qui commence à se
sentir un peu moins stable sur ses
pieds. La faiblesse des chevilles est
un sujet rarement abordé, et beaucoup
de seniors ignorent qu'elle augmente
discrètement les risques de chute
jusqu'à ce qu'il soit trop tard. Un
simple partage peut aider quelqu'un à
protéger sa confiance, sa sécurité
et son indépendance. Si cette vidéo
vous a aidé, écrivez « un » dans
les commentaires. Si quelque chose peut
être amélioré, écrivez « zéro »
et dites-moi ce que vous aimeriez que
j'explique plus clairement la prochaine
fois. Aimez, abonnez-vous et activez la
cloche de notification pour ne jamais
manquer la suite. À des chevilles plus
fortes, des pas plus assurés, des
matins plus sûrs et une vie vécue
selon vos propres termes. Merci d'avoir
regardé.

हूँ, शून्य
लिखें। आपके
टखने आपको
क्यों गिरा रहे
हैं। मुझे
समझाने दें कि
आपके टखने के
अंदर वास्तव
में क्या हो रहा
है। क्योंकि एक
बार जब आप इसे
समझ लेंगे, तो
मैं जो व्यायाम
आपको दिखाने
वाला हूँ, वे
पूरी तरह से समझ
में आ जाएंगे।
आपका टखने का
जोड़ छोटी
लेकिन बेहद
महत्वपूर्ण
मांसपेशियों,
टेंडन और
लिगामेंट्स के
एक नेटवर्क से
घिरा होता है।
उस पूरी संरचना
में हजारों
छोटे संवेदी
रिसेप्टर्स
बुने होते हैं
जिन्हें
प्रोप्रियोसेप्टर्स
कहा जाता है।
उन्हें
सूक्ष्म मोशन
सेंसर के रूप
में सोचें। हर
मिलीसेकंड, वे
आपके मस्तिष्क
को संकेत भेज
रहे होते हैं।
आपका पैर कहाँ
है, उस पर कितना
वजन है, जमीन
किस दिशा में
धक्का दे रही है
, और क्या आपका
शरीर केंद्र से
हट रहा है, इस
बारे में
जानकारी। आपका
मस्तिष्क उस
सारी जानकारी
को वास्तविक
समय में
प्रोसेस करता
है, और आपको
सीधा रखने के
लिए निर्देश
वापस भेजता है।
वह प्रणाली, जब
वह अच्छी तरह से
काम कर रही होती
है, तो असाधारण
होती है। यह
आपको गिरने का
एहसास होने से
पहले ही संभाल
लेती है। यह
आपकी किसी भी
सचेत प्रयास के
बिना, प्रति
मिनट दर्जनों
बार स्वचालित
रूप से सूक्ष्म
सुधार करती है।
लेकिन 70 की उम्र
के बाद क्या
होता है, वह
यहाँ है। पहला,
समतल और
अनुमानित
सतहों पर चलने
के वर्षों के
कारण टखने के
आसपास की
मांसपेशियां
कमजोर हो जाती
हैं, खासकर यदि
आप अपना
अधिकांश समय
मोटे, गद्देदार
जूतों में
बिताते हैं जो
आपके लिए
स्थिरता का
अधिकांश काम
करते हैं।
दूसरा, वे
प्रोप्रियोसेप्टिव
सेंसर, वे मोशन
डिटेक्टर उम्र
के साथ कम
संवेदनशील हो
जाते हैं। वे जो
संकेत आपके
मस्तिष्क को
भेजते हैं, वे
धीमे हो जाते
हैं। और तीसरा,
आपके मस्तिष्क
की उन संकेतों
को प्रोसेस
करने और जल्दी
से
प्रतिक्रिया
करने की क्षमता
भी कम हो जाती
है। परिणाम एक
ऐसी प्रणाली है
जो पहले एक
सेकंड के एक अंश
में ठोकर को ठीक
कर देती थी,
लेकिन अब उसे
प्रतिक्रिया
करने में थोड़ा
अधिक समय लगता
है। और बस वह
छोटी सी देरी ही
सब कुछ बिगाड़
देती है। मैं
इसे अपने
मरीजों को इस
तरह समझाता हूँ
। एक कार के शॉक
एब्जॉर्बर की
कल्पना करें जो
वर्षों से धीरे-
धीरे घिस रहे
हैं। कार अभी भी
चलती है। यह
आपको अभी भी
आपकी मंजिल तक
पहुंचाती है,
लेकिन सड़क पर
हर झटका जोर से
महसूस होता है।
हर अनपेक्षित
मोड़ थोड़ा कम
नियंत्रित
होता है। और एक
दिन आप एक ऐसे
झटके से टकराते
हैं जिसे
पुराने शॉक
एब्जॉर्बर
आसानी से संभाल
लेते, लेकिन अब
आप नहीं संभाल
पाते। सही
प्रशिक्षण के
बिना 70 की उम्र
के बाद आपके
टखने का यही हाल
होता है। सबसे
महत्वपूर्ण
बात जो मैं
चाहता हूँ कि आप
याद रखें, वह यह
है। कार्टिलेज
और हड्डियों के
घनत्व के
विपरीत, टखने की
ताकत और
प्रोप्रियोसेप्शन
, 80 और 90 के दशक
में भी लक्षित
व्यायाम के
प्रति बहुत
अच्छी
प्रतिक्रिया
देते हैं। ये
प्रशिक्षित
करने योग्य गुण
हैं। ये स्थायी
नुकसान नहीं
हैं। आपके
तंत्रिका
तंत्र ने यह
करना नहीं
भुलाया है। इसे
वापस जगाने के
लिए बस इसे
लगातार और सही
तरीके से
चुनौती देने की
आवश्यकता है।
ये पाँच
व्यायाम
बिल्कुल यही
करेंगे।
व्यायाम एक,
एड़ी से
वर्णमाला
लिखना। यह
क्यों मायने
रखता है।
ज्यादातर टखने
के व्यायाम पैर
को केवल एक या
दो दिशाओं में
ही हिलाते हैं,
लेकिन आपके
टखने को हर दिशा
में मजबूत और
प्रतिक्रियाशील
होने की
आवश्यकता है
क्योंकि
गिरावट हर दिशा
से आती है।
अल्फाबेट
ट्रेस आपके
टखने को उसकी
पूरी गति सीमा
में ले जाने के
सबसे प्रभावी
तरीकों में से
एक है, जो जोड़
के आसपास के हर
मांसपेशी समूह
को सक्रिय करता
है और
प्रोप्रियोसेप्टिव
सेंसर को जगाता
है जो वास्तविक
जीवन में आपकी
रक्षा करते हैं
। इसे कैसे करें
? एक मजबूत
कुर्सी पर
बैठें और अपने
पैरों को फर्श
पर सपाट रखें।
अपने दाहिने
पैर को जमीन से
कुछ इंच ऊपर
उठाएं। अपने
पैर को एक पेन
और अपने अंगूठे
को उसकी नोक
मानकर, हवा में
धीरे-धीरे
वर्णमाला का
प्रत्येक
अक्षर लिखें। ए,
बी, सी और इसी
तरह। हर अक्षर
को जितना संभव
हो उतना बड़ा
बनाएं। यह गति
पूरी तरह से
आपके टखने से
आनी चाहिए,
घुटने या
कूल्हे से नहीं
। दाहिने पैर पर
पूरी वर्णमाला
पूरी करें। फिर
बाएं पैर पर आ
जाएं। किस पर
ध्यान दें? धीरे
-धीरे और इरादे
के साथ चलें।
जितना बड़ा और
जानबूझकर
बनाया गया
अक्षर होगा,
उतनी ही अधिक
मांसपेशियों
की सक्रियता
आपको मिलेगी।
यदि पहले कुछ
अक्षरों में
आपका टखना सख्त
महसूस होता है,
तो यह पूरी तरह
से सामान्य है।
जैसे-जैसे आप
आगे बढ़ेंगे,
अकड़न कम हो
जाएगी। प्रगति
के लिए सुझाव।
समय के साथ, इस
व्यायाम को
आंखें बंद करके
करने का प्रयास
करें। दृश्य
इनपुट को हटाने
से आपकी
प्रोप्रियोसेप्टिव
प्रणाली को
अधिक मेहनत
करनी पड़ती है,
जिससे
न्यूरोलॉजिकल
प्रशिक्षण में
तेजी आती है।
व्यायाम दो, हील
वॉकिंग (एड़ी पर
चलना)। यह क्यों
महत्वपूर्ण है?
आपकी निचली
टांग के सामने
की मांसपेशी,
टिबियालिस
एंटीरियर,
गिरने से बचाव
में सबसे अधिक
अनदेखी की जाने
वाली
मांसपेशियों
में से एक है।
हर बार जब आप
कदम उठाने के
लिए अपना पैर
उठाते हैं, तो
यह मांसपेशी
नियंत्रित
करती है कि आपका
पैर कैसे उठता
है और कैसे जमीन
पर टिकता है। जब
यह कमजोर होती
है, तो आपका पैर
थोड़ा घिसटने
लगता है या
नियंत्रित
तरीके से टिकने
के बजाय जोर से
जमीन पर पड़ता
है, और यही
असमान जमीन पर
फिसलने और ठोकर
खाने के मुख्य
कारणों में से
एक है। हील
वॉकिंग सीधे इस
मांसपेशी को
लक्षित करती है
। इसे कैसे करें
? एक मजबूत
कुर्सी के पीछे
खड़े हों और
सहारे के लिए
अपने हाथों को
हल्के से पीठ पर
टिकाएं। दोनों
पैरों की
उंगलियों को
जमीन से ऊपर
उठाएं ताकि आप
पूरी तरह से
अपनी एड़ियों
पर संतुलन बना
सकें। इस
स्थिति में,
धीरे-धीरे आगे
चलें। अपनी
एड़ियों पर 10
छोटे कदम उठाएं,
उंगलियों को
पूरे समय ऊपर
रखें। फिर पीछे
की ओर 10 कदम चलें
। यह एक सेट हुआ
। दो सेट पूरे
करें। किस पर
ध्यान दें? अपने
कदम छोटे और
नियंत्रित
रखें।
जल्दबाजी न
करें। आप जितनी
धीमी गति से
चलेंगे, आपके
टिबियालिस
एंटीरियर को
उतना ही अधिक
काम करना होगा।
पूरे समय सीधे
खड़े रहें। आगे
न झुकें और न ही
अपने ऊपरी शरीर
को असंतुलित
होने दें।
प्रगति के लिए
सुझाव। जैसे-
जैसे यह आसान हो
जाए, कुर्सी से
अपनी पकड़ ढीली
करने की कोशिश
करें ताकि केवल
आपकी उंगलियां
ही उसे छुएं।
अंततः, बिना
किसी सहारे के
इसे करने का
प्रयास करें।
संतुलन के लिए
हाथों को अगल-
बगल फैलाएं।
व्यायाम तीन,
सिंगल लेग एंकल
सर्कल (एक पैर
पर टखने का
घुमाव)। यह
क्यों
महत्वपूर्ण है?
एक पैर पर खड़े
होकर दूसरे को
हिलाना सबसे
प्रभावी
संतुलन
चुनौतियों में
से एक है,
क्योंकि यह ठीक
वैसा ही है जैसा
आपका शरीर हर
कदम पर करता है।
हर कदम के दौरान
एक पल के लिए
आपके शरीर का
पूरा भार एक पैर
पर होता है। यह
व्यायाम खड़े
पैर के टखने को
भार के तहत
स्थिरता बनाए
रखने के लिए
प्रशिक्षित
करता है और साथ
ही दूसरे पैर की
गतिशीलता में
सुधार करता है।
गिरने से बचने
के लिए यह एक
बेहतरीन तरीका
है। इसे कैसे
करें? सहारे के
लिए दीवार या
कुर्सी के पास
खड़े हों। अपना
वजन अपने
दाहिने पैर पर
डालें और
दाहिने घुटने
को थोड़ा मुड़ा
हुआ रखें। इसे
कभी भी सीधा लॉक
न करें। धीरे से
अपने बाएं पैर
को जमीन से कुछ
इंच ऊपर उठाएं।
अब अपने बाएं
पैर को धीरे-
धीरे बड़े घेरों
में घुमाएं। 10
घेरे घड़ी की
दिशा में, फिर 10
घेरे विपरीत
दिशा में। अपने
दाहिने टखने को
पूरी
प्रक्रिया के
दौरान स्थिर
रखें। फिर
दूसरी तरफ
बदलें। अपने
बाएं पैर पर खड़े
हों और दाएं पैर
को घुमाएं।
दोनों तरफ दो-दो
राउंड पूरे
करें। किस पर
ध्यान दें? इस
व्यायाम का
मुख्य
प्रशिक्षण खड़े
पैर के टखने पर
हो रहा है, न कि
हिलने वाले पैर
पर। अपने खड़े
पैर को स्थिर
रखने, वजन को
बराबर बांटने
और घुटने को
थोड़ा लचीला
रखने पर ध्यान
दें। धीरे-धीरे
और गहराई से
सांस लें।
प्रगति के लिए
सुझाव। जब आप
स्थिर महसूस
करें, तो पूरा
हाथ हटाने के
बजाय एक उंगली
दीवार से हटाएं,
फिर दो
उंगलियां। समय
के साथ लक्ष्य
यह होना चाहिए
कि आप सतह को
पकड़ने के बजाय
हाथ को उसके पास
रखें, और जरूरत
पड़ने पर ही छुएं
। चौथा व्यायाम,
तौलिया
सिकोड़ना। यह
क्यों जरूरी है?
आपके पैर का
आर्च और
अंदरूनी
मांसपेशियां
सीधे आपके टखने
को स्थिर करने
की क्षमता से
जुड़ी होती हैं।
जब ये
मांसपेशियां
कमजोर होती हैं,
जो सालों तक
आरामदायक जूते
पहनने और सपाट
सतहों पर चलने
से होता है, तो
हर कदम पर आपका
पैर अंदर की ओर
झुक जाता है,
जिससे टखने पर
बुरा असर पड़ता
है। तौलिया
सिकोड़ने वाला
व्यायाम इन
गहरी
मांसपेशियों
को तुरंत
सक्रिय करता है
और उस आधार को
बहाल करता है
जिस पर आपका
टखना निर्भर है

text:
Falling while turning is one of the leading causes of serious injury in adults over 70 — and most people never see it coming. In this video, Dr. Thomas, a physical therapist with 26 years of experience, reveals a simple marching-step technique that eliminates the two most dangerous turning mistakes seniors make every day. Backed by balance science and biomechanics research, this easy method retrains your body to turn safely without crossing your feet or losing your center of gravity. No equipment needed. Just 30 seconds of practice can protect your independence for years to come.

Why turning is so dangerous.
Here's something most people don't
realize. Turning is one of the most
biomechanically complex movements we
make during normal daily activities.
When you're walking in a straight line,
your body settles into a rhythm. Your
weight is distributed evenly. Your
momentum is going in a predictable
direction, and your brain knows exactly
what to expect.
But the moment you turn, all of that

Your momentum is still carrying you
forward, but your body is trying to go
in a new direction. That mismatch
between where your momentum wants to

Add to that the fact that your feet can

I've seen it happen in my clinic, and
I've heard the stories from patients
time and again. Someone is walking

get crossed, and down they go.
The two biggest turning mistakes I see
again and again are
mistake number one,
turning too tight.
This is when someone tries to spin
around on a single spot, almost like
they're trying to turn on a dime.
When you do this, your legs can easily
cross over each other. Your feet get
tangled. Your center of gravity shifts
to one side, and that's when a fall
happens.
I've heard from so many patients who
fell exactly this way.
They went to turn, their legs crossed,
and there was nothing they could do to
stop it.
Mistake number two, taking too big of a
step. Some people try to compensate for
tight turning by swinging one leg out in
a wide arc to change direction.
The problem here is that a large

gravity way outside of your body. Your
balance is compromised, and if you're
moving with any momentum at all, that
wide step can send you tumbling to one
side. This mistake is just as dangerous
as turning too tight, it just looks
different.
The solution to both of these problems

The marching turn, your number one tool
for turning safely.
The marching turn sounds a little
unusual at first, but when you actually
do it, it feels natural. It looks
normal, and most importantly, it works.
Here's the concept. Instead of crossing
your legs over each other to turn,
either tightly or with a big step, you
use small controlled marching steps to
gradually rotate your body in the new
direction.
Here's how to practice it.
One, stand in a comfortable, stable
position with your feet about hip width
apart.
Two, decide you want to turn. Let's say
90° to your right.
Three, instead of swinging your right
foot across your body or pivoting
sharply, lift your right knee slightly.
Just a small controlled march step.
Four, as you step down, allow your body
to rotate about 30° to the right.
Five, lift the left knee, step, rotate
another 30°.
Six, continue this small marching motion
until you've completed your turn.
At no point in this movement do your
legs cross over each other. At no point
does your center of gravity shoot out to
one side. You are always in control,
always balanced, always safe.
Now, I'll be honest, when you first

natural walking pace, it looks

The key things to remember about the
marching turn.
Step up and forward, not across. Your
feet should never cross the midline of
your body.
Rotate about 30° per step. Smaller turns
mean more steps, but more steps mean
more stability.
Use your ankle muscles.
Let your ankles and feet do the rotating
work, not your hips or momentum.
Take your time. There is no rush. A safe
turn is always better than a fast one.
Practice this turn in your home every
day.
Walk down the hallway, get to the end,
and use the marching turn to come back.
Do it in the kitchen. Do it in the

more automatic it becomes, and the safer

Five supporting exercises to make
turning even safer.
The marching turn is your primary tool,
but like any tool, it works best when
the person using it is strong and
prepared. The following five exercises
are specifically designed to build the
strength, balance, and coordination that
makes safe turning possible.
Add these to your daily routine and
you'll be amazed at the difference they
make.
Exercise one, standing heel raises.
Why it matters. Your calf muscles and
ankles are your first line of defense
against falls. Strong ankles absorb
uneven ground,
adjust to changes in direction, and keep
you upright when your balance is
challenged. This exercise directly
targets that area.
How to do it.
Stand behind a sturdy chair and hold the
back lightly for balance.
Place your feet hip-width apart, toes
pointing forward.
Slowly rise up onto the balls of your
feet as high as you comfortably can.
Hold at the top for 2 seconds.
Slowly lower your heels back down to the
floor.
That's one rep. Complete two sets of 12
to 15 repetitions.
What to focus on.
Keep the movement slow and controlled,
especially on the way down. The lowering
phase is just as important as the
lifting phase for building ankle
strength.
Progress tip, as you get stronger, try
doing one leg at a time. Hold the chair
for safety and do eight to 10 reps on
each side.
Exercise two,
side-to-side weight shifts.
Why it matters. When you turn, your
weight shifts from one foot to the
other. If your body isn't practiced at
controlling that lateral shift, a turn
can easily throw you off balance. This
exercise trains your brain and your legs
to manage side-to-side weight changes
safely.
How to do it.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width
apart with a chair or countertop nearby
for support.
Slowly shift your weight to your right
foot, lifting your left foot slightly
off the ground, just a half inch or so.
Hold for 3 to 5 seconds, keeping your
right knee soft, not locked.
Slowly shift back to center, then to
your left foot.
Hold for 3 to 5 seconds.
That's one full rep. Complete two sets
of 10 repetitions on each side.
What to focus on. Keep your standing
knee slightly bent. Don't lock it. Think
about keeping your core gently engaged.
Imagine someone is about to tap your
shoulder from the side and you're
bracing yourself.
Progress tip. Try doing this with your
eyes closed once you feel steady.
Removing visual input forces your
balance system to work harder and get
stronger.
Exercise three, marching in place. Why
it matters. The marching turn depends on
your ability to lift your knees with
control while staying balanced. This
exercise builds exactly that skill. It
also improves hip flexor strength, leg
coordination, and the connection between
your brain and your feet, all of which
decline with age and must be actively
maintained.
How to do it. Stand behind a chair,
holding it lightly for balance.
Begin marching in place, lifting each
knee to a comfortable height, ideally to
about hip level, but go as high as is
comfortable for you.
March at a slow, controlled pace. Count
one full left-right cycle as one rep.
Complete two sets of 20 steps, 10 per
side.
What to focus on.
Don't rush. Keep your torso upright.
Don't lean forward or let your back
round. Each step should be deliberate
and controlled.
Progress
tip. Once you feel comfortable, practice
the full marching turn movement during
this exercise.
Walk forward a few steps, march turn to
the left or right, walk a few more
steps, turn again.
You're now practicing the exact skill
you need for daily life.
Exercise four, tandem standing,
tightrope balance. Why it matters. The
most vulnerable moment during a turn is
that split second when your weight is
transitioning from one foot to the other
on a narrow base.
Tandem standing, placing one foot
directly in front of the other, trains
your body to manage exactly this kind of
narrow, unstable base.
It's one of the most effective balance
exercises available and it requires no
equipment.
How to do it.
Stand next to a wall or counter top for
safety.
Place your right foot directly in front
of your left foot so that the heel of
your right foot is touching the toes of
your left foot. This is called the
tandem position.
Hold this position for 20 to 30 seconds,
trying not to touch the wall unless
necessary.
Switch so your left foot is in front and
hold again for 20 to 30 seconds.
Complete two sets on each side.
What to focus on. Keep your gaze fixed

A steady visual focus point dramatically

happen when we reach, twist, and turn

hip strength, and the dynamic balance

movements like turning while carrying
something.

Stand on your right foot next to a chair
holding it lightly with your right hand
for safety.
Imagine you're standing in the center of

back to center.
Reach to 10:00, slightly to the left,
return.
Reach to 9:00, directly to your side,
return.
Reach to 7:00, diagonally behind you,
return.

Eventually, try just hovering your

One. Heel raises.
Two sets of 12 to 15 reps.
Two.

Six, marching turn.
Practice.
Walk a short route around your home and

Consistency is the secret here. You

Who I am and why this matters.
My name is Dr. Thomas and I'm a physical
therapist with 26 years of experience
helping adults over 50 move better, feel
stronger, and live with more confidence.
Throughout my career, I've had the honor
of working with thousands of patients,
helping them get back on their feet,
rebuild their independence, and stop

Turning.

Because turning is something we all do
dozens of times a day without a second
thought. And for many people over 70,

If I can help you move through that

A final word on staying safe.
I want to leave you with this thought.

That distinction matters because the

The goal is to make you more capable.
After 26 years of working with patients

After 60, poor leg circulation is one of the most common — and most overlooked — health concerns in older adults. If your legs feel heavy, swollen, or exhausted by midday, your calf muscles may have quietly stopped working as your body's natural venous pump.
