ज्यादा कठिन है,
और यही इसका
मुख्य
उद्देश्य है।
चौथा व्यायाम,
खड़े होकर
मार्च करना। जब
आप किसी चीज से
टकराते हैं,
जैसे गलीचा,
सीढ़ी या
फुटपाथ की दरार,
तो आपके शरीर को
बाधा को पार
करने के लिए
अपने पैर को
जल्दी और
पर्याप्त ऊपर
उठाने की जरूरत
होती है। यदि
आपकी हिप
फ्लेक्सर्स
मांसपेशियां
कमजोर हैं और
पैर उठाने की
प्रतिक्रिया
धीमी है, तो
ठोकर लगने पर
गिरना निश्चित
हो जाता है।
खड़े होकर
मार्च करना
सीधे इसी पर काम
करता है। अपनी
कुर्सी के पीछे
सीधे खड़े हो
जाएं, सहारे के
लिए हाथ हल्के
से कुर्सी पर
रखें। अपने
दाहिने घुटने
को धीरे-धीरे
अपनी छाती की ओर
उतना ऊपर उठाएं
जितना आप बिना
अपने शरीर को
पीछे झुकाए
आराम से कर सकें
। ऊपर की स्थिति
में दो सेकंड तक
रुकें। फिर इसे
धीरे-धीरे वापस
जमीन पर ले आएं।
बाईं ओर से
दोहराएं। यह एक
रेपुटेशन है।
दोनों तरफ 10 बार
दोहराएं। ऊपर
और नीचे जाते
समय यह गतिविधि
धीमी और
नियंत्रित
होनी चाहिए।
जल्दबाजी न
करें। नीचे ले
जाने का चरण ऊपर
उठाने के चरण
जितना ही
महत्वपूर्ण है
क्योंकि यह
मांसपेशियों
का वह संतुलन
बनाता है जो
जमीन पर पैर
रखते समय आपको
स्थिर रखता है।
जैसे-जैसे यह
आसान हो जाए,
इसे बिना
कुर्सी पकड़े
करने का प्रयास
करें। इसके
बजाय संतुलन के
लिए भुजाओं को
अगल-बगल फैलाएं
। पांचवां
व्यायाम।
क्लॉक रीचेस (
घड़ी की दिशा
में पहुंचना)।
यह व्यायाम '
मल्टीडायरेक्शनल
बैलेंस'(बहु-
दिशात्मक
संतुलन) के
प्रशिक्षण के
लिए सबसे अच्छे
व्यायामों में
से एक है।
विभिन्न
दिशाओं में
पहुंचने,
खिंचाव करने और
हिलने-डुलने की
आपकी क्षमता
बिना संतुलन
खोए। दिन भर में
उन सभी पलों के
बारे में सोचें
जब आप किसी चीज
के लिए हाथ
बढ़ाते हैं।
ऊपर की अलमारी,
कॉफी पॉट, या
अपने पोते-पोती
को उठाना।
उनमें से हर पल
एक संतुलन की
चुनौती है।
अपनी कुर्सी के
पीछे खड़े हों
और अपना दाहिना
हाथ हल्के से
पीठ पर रखें।
कल्पना करें कि
आप फर्श पर घड़ी
के केंद्र में
खड़े हैं। धीरे-
धीरे अपने बाएं
पैर को 12 बजे की
दिशा में आगे
बढ़ाएं और अपने
पंजों को धीरे
से फर्श पर छुएं
। केंद्र में
वापस आएं। अब 9
बजे की दिशा में
सीधे बाईं ओर
पहुंचें। वापस
आएं। अब पीछे 7
बजे की दिशा में
थोड़ा बाईं ओर
पहुंचें। वापस
आएं। यह एक
राउंड है। बाएं
पैर से तीन
राउंड करें।
फिर बदल लें।
कुर्सी को अपने
बाएं हाथ से
पकड़ें और अपने
दाहिने पैर से 12,
3 और 5 बजे की
दिशा में
पहुंचें। पूरे
समय अपने खड़े
रहने वाले
पैरों को थोड़ा
मुड़ा हुआ रखें
और अपनी पीठ
सीधी रखें। यह
व्यायाम एक पैर
पर स्थिरता,
कूल्हे की
मजबूती और टखने
पर नियंत्रण
बनाता है जो एक
साथ गिरने से
रोकता है। छठा
व्यायाम, हाथों
का उपयोग किए
बिना बैठकर
खड़े होना। यह
जानकर बहुतों
को हैरानी होती
है। 70 साल से
अधिक उम्र के
किसी भी
व्यक्ति के लिए
कुर्सी से उठना
गिरने के सबसे
जोखिम भरे
क्षणों में से
एक है। और फिर
भी, ज़्यादातर
लोग इसका विशेष
रूप से अभ्यास
कभी नहीं करते।
यह व्यायाम
दोहरे लाभ देता
है। यह पैरों की
ताकत बढ़ाता है
और साथ ही आपके
संतुलन को भी
बेहतर बनाता है,
जिससे यह
रोज़मर्रा की
ज़िंदगी में
सुरक्षित रहने
के सबसे
व्यावहारिक
तरीकों में से
एक बन जाता है।
एक मज़बूत
कुर्सी के अगले
किनारे पर
बैठें, पैर
ज़मीन पर सपाट
और कूल्हों की
चौड़ाई जितनी
दूरी पर रखें।
अपनी भुजाओं को
अपनी छाती पर
क्रॉस करें।
इससे हाथों के
सहारे उठने का
प्रलोभन खत्म
हो जाता है।
अपने ऊपरी शरीर
को कूल्हों से
थोड़ा आगे की ओर
झुकाएँ, नाक को
पंजों के ऊपर
रखें, और फिर
धीरे-धीरे और
नियंत्रण के
साथ खड़े होने
के लिए अपनी
एड़ियों पर
ज़ोर दें। एक
बार जब आप पूरी
तरह खड़े हो
जाएँ, तो दो
सेकंड रुकें,
फिर धीरे-धीरे
वापस बैठने की
स्थिति में आएँ
। कुर्सी पर
धड़ाम से न
बैठें। नीचे
बैठने की पूरी
प्रक्रिया को
नियंत्रित
रखें। यह एक बार
(रिप) हुआ। आठ
बार दोहराने से
शुरुआत करें।
यदि शुरुआत में
बिना हाथों के
यह बहुत कठिन लग
रहा है, तो कोई
बात नहीं।
हल्के सहारे के
लिए अपने हाथ
जांघों पर रखें
और धीरे-धीरे
समय के साथ उनका
उपयोग कम करते
जाएँ। लक्ष्य
अंततः बिना
किसी हाथ के
सहारे के पूरे
नियंत्रण के
साथ उठना और
बैठना है। अब,
इन सभी छह
व्यायामों का
उपयोग करने का
सबसे अच्छा
तरीका वह है
जिसे मैं '
बैलेंस
एक्सरसाइज़
स्नैक्स' कहता
हूँ।
प्रशिक्षण के
छोटे-छोटे
अंतराल, केवल 30
से 60 सेकंड के,
जिन्हें एक बार
में करने के
बजाय पूरे दिन
में फैलाया जाए
। कॉफी बनते समय
'टो लीन'(पंजों
पर झुकाव) करें।
टीवी पर
विज्ञापन के
ब्रेक के दौरान
'वेट शिफ्ट'(
वज़न बदलना)
करें। दोपहर के
भोजन से पहले '
सिट टू
स्टैंड्स'(
बैठकर उठना)
करें।
माइक्रोवेव का
इंतज़ार करते
समय 'स्टैंडिंग
मार्च'(खड़े
होकर कदमताल)
करें। यह
वास्तविक जीवन
में इस तरह फिट
बैठता है जैसे
जिम का लंबा
सत्र कभी नहीं
हो सकता। और शोध
भी वृद्ध
वयस्कों में
संतुलन और
समन्वय को फिर
से बनाने के लिए
इस वितरित
दृष्टिकोण का
पुरज़ोर
समर्थन करता है
। दिन भर में
लगातार दोहराई
जाने वाली छोटी-
छोटी खुराकें
आपके तंत्रिका
तंत्र को एक
शक्तिशाली
संकेत भेजती
हैं और आपका
शरीर
प्रतिक्रिया
करता है। आपको
शुरुआत से ही हर
दिन सभी छह
व्यायाम करने
की ज़रूरत नहीं
है। यह बहुत
अधिक हो जाएगा
और मैं नहीं
चाहता कि आप
पहले ही हफ़्ते
में थक जाएँ और
छोड़ दें। इसके
बजाय, इसे एक
क्रमिक प्रगति
के रूप में लें।
केवल 'टो लीन' और
'साइड टू साइड
वेट शिफ्ट' से
शुरुआत करें।
उन दो का तब तक
अभ्यास करें जब
तक कि वे
स्वाभाविक न
लगें, जब तक आप
दीवार को न
पकड़ें, और जब
तक आप वास्तव
में स्थिर
महसूस न करें।
इसमें कुछ दिन
लग सकते हैं।
इसमें एक या दो
हफ़्ते भी लग
सकते हैं।
दोनों ही तरह से
बिल्कुल ठीक है
। एक बार जब वे
ठोस लगने लगें,
तो 'हील टू टो
वॉक' जोड़ें,
फिर 'स्टैंडिंग
मार्च', फिर '
क्लॉक रीच', और
अंत में 'सिट टू
स्टैंड्स'
जोड़ें। हर
हफ्ते लगभग एक
नया व्यायाम
जोड़ें, उतनी ही
गति से जितनी
आपका शरीर
अनुमति दे। छह
सप्ताह के अंत
तक, आपके पास एक
संपूर्ण दैनिक
संतुलन
दिनचर्या होगी
जिसमें 10 मिनट
से भी कम समय
लगेगा, और आप
वर्षों की
तुलना में अपने
पैरों पर अधिक
मजबूत, स्थिर और
आत्मविश्वासी
महसूस करेंगे।
और कृपया उन
दिनों में इन
अभ्यासों को न
छोड़ें जब आप
बहुत अच्छा
महसूस कर रहे
हों। मैं जानता
हूँ कि यह
लुभावना है। जब
आप स्थिर महसूस
करते हैं, तो यह
सोचना आसान है
कि आज परेशान
होने की जरूरत
नहीं है, लेकिन
वास्तव में वही
दिन सबसे
महत्वपूर्ण
होते हैं। हर एक
दोहराव उस
प्रतिवर्त (reflex)
का निर्माण कर
रहा है जो अगली
बार लड़खड़ाने
पर स्वचालित
रूप से सक्रिय
हो जाएगा, और
गिरने का एहसास
होने से पहले ही
आपको संभाल
लेगा। आप अभी
मेहनत कर रहे
हैं ताकि बाद
में उस
महत्वपूर्ण पल
में आपका शरीर
आपकी रक्षा कर
सके। आज हमने जो
कुछ भी कवर किया
है, उसका पूरा
सार यही है। यह
केवल गिरने से
बचाने के बारे
में नहीं है। यह
आपकी
स्वतंत्रता की
रक्षा करने के
बारे में है। यह
आपके दिन भर
बिना किसी दबे
हुए डर के चलने
के बारे में है।
यह चीजों तक
पहुँचने, बाहर
कदम रखने और जब
तक संभव हो अपने
घर में अपनी
शर्तों पर अपना
जीवन पूरी तरह
जीने के बारे
में है। अब,
संतुलन गिरने
से बचाव के
समीकरण का केवल
एक आधा हिस्सा
है। दूसरा आधा
हिस्सा आपके
पैरों की ताकत
है। और यह ऐसी
चीज है जिसे मैं
चाहता हूँ कि आप
बहुत गंभीरता
से लें क्योंकि
बहुत से लोग
पूरी तरह से
संतुलन पर
ध्यान
केंद्रित करते
हैं और इस दूसरे
हिस्से को पूरी
तरह से अनदेखा
कर देते हैं। और
यह एक महंगी
गलती है।
अनुसंधान
वास्तव में यह
दिखाता है।
मजबूत पैरों
वाले लोगों की
तुलना में
कमजोर पैरों
वाले लोगों के
किसी भी वर्ष
में गिरने की
संभावना पांच
गुना अधिक होती
है। पांच गुना।
इस संख्या को
गहराई से समझें
। यह कोई छोटा
अंतर नहीं है।
कमजोर पैरों का
मतलब है
लड़खड़ाने पर
धीमी
प्रतिक्रिया
समय। इसका मतलब
है कि जब आपका
शरीर गलत दिशा
में झुकता है तो
पीछे धकेलने के
लिए कम शक्ति।
इसका मतलब है
आपके द्वारा
उठाए गए हर कदम
के साथ आपके
कूल्हों और
घुटनों में कम
स्थिरता। और
समय के साथ, वह
कमजोरी चुपचाप
आपके
आत्मविश्वास,
आपके आसन और
आपके दिन भर
स्वतंत्र रूप
से घूमने की
क्षमता को कम कर
देती है। उन
रोजमर्रा के
क्षणों के बारे
में सोचें जो
पैरों की ताकत
पर निर्भर करते
हैं। सोफे से
उठना, सीढ़ी
चढ़ना,
पार्किंग में
चलना, ठोकर लगने
पर खुद को
संभालना।
उनमें से हर पल
के लिए आपके
पैरों को जल्दी
और मजबूती से
प्रतिक्रिया
देने की
आवश्यकता होती
है। जब वे ऐसा
नहीं कर पाते
हैं, तो गंभीर
रूप से गिरने का
जोखिम तेजी से

stützen diesen verteilten Ansatz zum
Aufbau von Gleichgewicht und

Kleine, über den Tag konsistent

Signal an Ihr Nervensystem, auf das der
Körper reagiert. Sie müssen nicht von
Anfang an jeden Tag alle sechs Übungen
machen. Das wäre zu viel, und ich
möchte nicht, dass Sie in der ersten
Woche ausbrennen und aufgeben.
Betrachten Sie es stattdessen als einen
schrittweisen Aufbau. Beginnen Sie nur
mit dem Zehen-Lehnen und den seitlichen
Gewichtsverlagerungen. Üben Sie diese
beiden, bis sie sich natürlich
anfühlen, bis Sie nicht mehr nach der
Wand greifen müssen und sich wirklich
stabil fühlen. Das kann ein paar Tage
dauern. Vielleicht dauert es ein oder
zwei Wochen. Beides ist völlig in
Ordnung. Wenn diese sicher sitzen,
nehmen Sie das Gehen auf der Linie,
dann den Stand-Marsch, die Uhr-Reich-
Übung und schließlich das Aufstehen
dazu. Fügen Sie etwa jede Woche eine
neue Übung hinzu, ganz in dem Tempo,
das Ihr Körper zulässt. Nach sechs
Wochen haben Sie ein vollständiges
tägliches Gleichgewichtstraining, das
insgesamt weniger als 10 Minuten dauert
, und Sie werden sich stärker,
standfester und trittsicherer fühlen
als seit Jahren. Und bitte lassen Sie
diese Übungen an den Tagen, an denen
Sie sich großartig fühlen, nicht aus.
Ich weiß, es ist verlockend. Wenn man
sich sicher fühlt, denkt man leicht,
dass man sich heute nicht anstrengen
muss, aber das sind tatsächlich die
wichtigsten Tage überhaupt. Jede
einzelne Wiederholung trainiert den
Reflex, der beim nächsten Stolpern
automatisch einsetzt und Sie auffängt,
noch bevor Sie merken, dass Sie fallen.
Sie leisten jetzt die Arbeit, damit Ihr
Körper Sie später in dem
Sekundenbruchteil schützen kann, in
dem es am wichtigsten ist. Das ist der
eigentliche Sinn von allem, was wir
heute besprochen haben. Es geht nicht
nur darum, Stürze zu vermeiden. Es
geht darum, Ihre Unabhängigkeit zu
bewahren. Es geht darum, Ihren Tag zu
verbringen, ohne diese leise Angst im
Hinterkopf. Es geht darum, nach Dingen
zu greifen, nach draußen zu gehen und
Ihr Leben so lange wie möglich
selbstbestimmt in Ihrem eigenen Zuhause
zu führen. Gleichgewicht ist jedoch
nur die eine Hälfte der Gleichung zur
Sturzprävention. Die andere Hälfte
ist Ihre Beinkraft. Und das ist etwas,
das ich Sie sehr ernst nehmen möchte,
denn viele Menschen konzentrieren sich
nur auf das Gleichgewicht und
übersehen diesen zweiten Teil völlig.

tatsächlich zeigt. Menschen mit
schwachen Beinen stürzen in einem Jahr
mehr als fünfmal häufiger als

Reaktionszeiten, wenn Sie ins Stolpern
geraten. Sie bedeuten weniger Kraft, um
gegenzusteuern, wenn Ihr Körper in die

weniger Stabilität in Ihren Hüften
und Knien bei jedem einzelnen Schritt,

und Ihrer Fähigkeit, sich frei durch
den Tag zu bewegen. Denken Sie an die
alltäglichen Momente, die von
Beinkraft abhängen. Vom Sofa aufstehen
, eine Stufe steigen, über einen
Parkplatz laufen, sich beim Stolpern
abfangen. In all diesen Momenten

kraftvoll reagieren. Wenn sie das nicht

schweren Sturzes rapide an. Und die

reagieren. Sie haben noch nicht
aufgegeben. Sie warten nur auf das
richtige Signal. Und selbst bescheidene

durch einfache Übungen zu Hause
mehrmals pro Woche entstehen, können
einen dramatischen Unterschied bei
Ihrem Sturzrisiko, Ihrer Stabilität
und Ihrem täglichen Selbstvertrauen
bewirken. Genau deshalb habe ich ein

text:
Prolonged sitting is one of the most overlooked circulation threats for older adults. When you stay seated for hours, your calf muscles — the body's natural "second heart" — stop pumping blood back toward your heart, dramatically raising your risk of deep vein thrombosis and dangerous blood clots. In this video, a vascular surgeon with 26 years of experience shares 5 gentle chair exercises that reactivate your calf muscle pump, reduce leg swelling, and improve circulation — no walking required. Safe for seniors with knee pain or limited mobility. Do this 8–10 minute routine 2–3 times daily to protect your legs and your life.

lebih bermanfaat daripada 15 repetisi

. Putaran pergelangan kaki, 10 kali

text:
Many adults over 60 dismiss early stroke symptoms because they disappear within minutes — but those brief episodes may be the most important warning your brain ever sends you. In this video, I walk you through five medically recognized signs that often appear hours or days before a major stroke, explain exactly what is happening inside your blood vessels when they occur, and tell you which three clinical tests can help your doctor assess your real risk. Understanding these signals could be the difference between prevention and permanent disability. If you or someone you love is over 60, this information belongs in your hands now.

What if I told you that your brain may
have already sent you a warning that a
stroke was coming and you completely
missed it?
Every 40 seconds, somewhere on this
planet, someone has a stroke. By the
time you finish reading this sentence,
another brain has been hit. Every year,
stroke kills almost 6 million people
worldwide, ranks as the second leading
cause of death, and is the number one
reason people end up with permanent
disability.
The part nobody tells you clearly
enough, in a huge number of cases, the
brain gives you very specific warnings
hours or even days before the big stroke
happens.
You just have to know what they look
like.
Before we dive in, if you haven't
subscribed yet, I recommend you hit that
button and turn on the bell so you never
miss another health tip made just for
you.
If you enjoy this video, type one in the
comments. If not, type zero to let me
know how I can make better content for
you.
Stroke is not just you were fine, you
fell, you woke up in the hospital. In
most cases, stroke is the predictable
endpoint of blood vessels that have been
degrading for years. If something is
predictable, it is at least partly
preventable. That is the whole point of
what I'm sharing with you today.
Two very different events.
When people say stroke, they are
actually talking about two very
different events in the brain.
One is a hemorrhagic stroke. A blood
vessel in the brain bursts. Blood pours
into or around the brain, forms a clot
that compresses brain tissue, and a lot
of those patients die.
The other is an ischemic stroke. A
vessel does not tear, but gets blocked.
Blood flow stops to part of the brain,
and brain cells in that zone start dying
in roughly 4 to 6 minutes. Ischemic
strokes make up around 85% of all
strokes. So, that is what I'm going to
focus on today.
To understand why every minute matters,
you need a feel for how demanding your
brain actually is. Your brain weighs
roughly 1.4 kg, about 2% of your body
weight, but it uses around 20% of the
oxygen you breathe in and about 25% of
all the glucose circulating in your
blood.
It is a control center that never turns
off and it needs a constant fuel line.
Cut that fuel for even a few minutes and
cells start dying in ways you cannot
reverse. That is why doctors say stroke
is a race against time. It is literally
a race to save brain tissue before it is
gone for good.
The groundwork was laid years ago.
Most people miss what I'm about to say.
For a brain artery to suddenly block,
the groundwork usually took years. The
walls of the vessel have been damaged,
material and clots have been building up
and the opening has been getting
tighter. This is not an explosion out of
nowhere. It is the last step of a long
process.
Along that road, your body usually sends
out warning signals. The problem is
nobody ever taught you how to read them.
In medicine, those early warning shots
are called a transient ischemic attack,
or TIA for short. Transient just means
temporary. It comes and it goes. Picture
a carotid artery, the main neck artery
that carries blood from your heart up to
your brain. Over years, a fatty plaque
forms on the inner wall right where the
artery branches. The opening slowly
narrows. Then at some point, the already
tight vessel goes into a brief spasm.
Blood flow stops for a few seconds or a
few minutes, and the brain area fed by
that artery basically blacks out for
that short time. You see or feel a
stroke symptom, then the spasm relaxes,
blood flow returns, and the symptom
fades, and you think you are fine again.
What research actually shows is that a
transient ischemic attack very often
comes right before a major ischemic
stroke, typically within the next 72
hours. Those three days are your window
where the disaster can still be
prevented. Most people do not use that
window because the warning episode was
short, strange, and then went away. So,
they talk themselves out of taking it
seriously.
These warning episodes usually last from
about half a minute to maybe 10 minutes.
That is exactly why they slip through
the cracks. You can be in your kitchen,
in the shower, getting out of a car, and
by the time you stop and think, the
symptom has already passed. But, each of
those episodes is your brain sending a
final very clear message, "I am about to
be in serious trouble."
I want to walk you through the five big
red flags and explain not just what they
look like, but what is actually
happening inside your body each time.
Warning sign number one, temporary
blindness in one eye.
You get up, walk toward the kitchen, and
suddenly one eye goes dark or foggy,
like someone pulled down a black curtain
over that eye or smeared the lens with
gray mud. You blink a few times, maybe
rub the eye, and within seconds or a
minute at most, your vision comes back.
So, you blame it on standing up too fast
or too much screen time.
In reality, that curtain is almost
always a tiny clot or a small fragment
of plaque that broke off from the wall
of your carotid artery, traveled up, and
briefly plugged the artery that feeds
the eye.
The artery to your eye is not some
random isolated tube. It is a direct
branch of the inner carotid artery that
feeds your brain. When the clot or
plaque fragment wedges into that tiny
eye artery, blood cannot get through.
So, the retina, the light-sensing
tissue, loses its blood supply for a
moment, and you see darkness or a smear
instead of a clear image.
When the clot drifts away and blood flow
restarts, the vision comes back and you
feel lucky. You were lucky because that
exact same clot could have gone 2 mm to
the side into a brain artery and then
instead of a 1-minute blackout in one
eye, you are looking at permanent loss
of speech, paralysis of an arm and leg,
or death.
Doctors have a classic name for that
one-eye blackout, amaurosis fugax, which
literally means fleeting blindness.
Neurologists treat that phrase like a
fire alarm. If a patient describes an
episode like that, they get urgent
evaluation because the risk of a real
stroke in the next hours is high.
Hospital records show a pattern where a
person ignores two or three of these eye
episodes and the very next one is the
big one in the brain.
Warning sign number two, sudden numbness
or tingling on one side.
The medical word is paresthesia, but you
can think of it as your skin acting
drunk. It can be the whole arm, just the
hand, half the face, or even one full
side of the body.
It feels like pins and needles, like
cotton, or like that body part has
turned into rubber.
The key detail is that it comes out of
nowhere while you are just sitting,
walking, or talking, lasts a few
minutes, then goes away on its own.
You have probably slept on your arm at
some point where nerve compression
causes numbness that clears up when you
move.
That is different. There, your brain and
spinal cord are fine. You squeezed a
nerve and as soon as blood flow and
position normalize, sensation returns in
a minute or two.
With a TIA, the problem is not in the
arm. It is in the brain area that maps
sensation from that arm and the episode
has nothing to do with posture.
One more thing worth knowing. Stroke
symptoms are usually one-sided because
each brain hemisphere controls and feels
the opposite side of your body. When
both hands go numb evenly, that more
often points to neck spine issues. But a
sudden one-sided numbness that resolves
after a few minutes is a strong reason
to get checked for TIA and stroke risk.
Warning sign number three, sudden loss
of coordination, the drunk walk.
You are on a flat familiar surface and
out of nowhere, your foot lands in the
wrong place. Your leg feels weak or
rubbery or you stagger into the wall for
a second. Or you get hit by a sudden
strong spinning sensation that makes you
grab a chair or the doorframe even
though you were not spinning, you did
not jerk your head and you did not just
stand up from bed.
The part of your brain that keeps you
balanced and coordinates smooth movement
is called the cerebellum. It sits low in
the back of your skull like a small
extra brain. It constantly calculates
where your body is in space and how hard
each muscle should fire so you walk
straight instead of zigzagging. The
cerebellum gets its blood supply from
arteries that run up through the bones
of your neck into the back of your head,
what doctors call the vertebrobasilar
system.
If blood flow in those arteries drop
sharply, even for a few seconds, the
cerebellum essentially glitches. That is
when you suddenly veer sideways,
misstep, or feel violent dizziness for
no obvious reason.
In clinical practice, I have seen a
pattern where people write off these
episodes as bad shoes, being tired, or
high blood pressure, only to find out
later that those were cerebellar
transient attacks.
Benign dizziness usually has a clear
trigger, rolling over in bed, turning
the head quickly, a known inner ear
condition. But spontaneous intense
dizziness plus any trouble walking
straight should be treated as a possible
TIA until a doctor rules out a vascular
cause.
Warning sign number four, speech that
suddenly breaks down.
Before we go further, I want to be clear
about something. If you occasionally
cannot remember your neighbor's name or
you temporarily forget the word for
toothbrush, that is not a stroke sign.
That is a normal tip of the tongue
moment that happens more when you are
tired or stressed.
What worries neurologists is something
quite different. When your speech
suddenly breaks down so badly that even
you feel something is seriously wrong.
There are two main speech areas in most
people's brains, both usually in the
left hemisphere. One area, often called
Broca's area, helps you form words and
send clear instructions to the muscles
of your tongue, lips, and jaw. When that
region loses blood flow, you may
understand everything people say, you
know what you want to answer, but you
cannot get the words out. They come out
slurred, chopped, or stuck.
The other area, often called Wernicke's
area, helps you understand speech and
organize your own sentences so they make
sense. When that zone is in trouble, a
person may speak fluently but say
complete nonsense, like word salad, and
may not understand simple phrases
directed at them.
If any of those speech problems show up
suddenly and then fade after a few
minutes, that is classic for a TIA, not
I was just tired. You cannot ignore
broken speech just because it
self-corrected. That is like your home
alarm going off, stopping by itself, and
you deciding it was probably nothing.
Warning sign number five, vitiligo
combined with new unusually strong
headaches.
The fifth warning sign is less obvious
and surprises most people. It is a
combination of certain skin changes plus
new unusually strong headaches.
The skin condition is vitiligo, patches
of pale or completely white skin where
pigment-producing cells have stopped
working. Vitiligo is an autoimmune
process, meaning the immune system
starts attacking your own pigment cells
as if they were foreign. When your
immune system goes off target like that,
it often does not stop at one organ. In
many people, that same autoimmune
process can quietly inflame the inner
lining of blood vessels as well. That
inner lining is called the endothelium,
a microscopically thin layer of cells
that coats the inside of every artery
like a super smooth nonstick surface.
When the endothelium is healthy, blood
components glide by and nothing really
sticks. When it is damaged by
inflammation, it becomes rough and
scarred and things start to cling,
cholesterol, platelets, various
inflammatory proteins, forming the seeds
of plaques and clots over time.
Vitiligo alone does not doom you to a
stroke, but if on top of that you
develop frequent, unusually intense
headaches that do not fit your usual
pattern, that combination deserves a
proper vascular workup rather than a
wait-and-see approach.
Headaches in general are tricky because
a lot of people blame blood vessel
problems when the real issue is
elsewhere. A very common cause of daily
or frequent head pain is wear and tear
in the small joints between the second
and third neck vertebrae. Basically,
arthritis in the neck. That joint
degeneration can irritate nearby nerves
and send pain up into the head, which
has nothing to do with a brain artery
being blocked. On top of that, many
people carry an undiagnosed neck disc
herniation. And if you never address it,
in severe cases it can threaten the
nerve supply to your arms or legs.
Headaches should not just be numbed with
pills long-term. They need to be decoded
with a doctor, especially when they
change character or pair up with other
warning signs like the ones we just
covered.
What to do if you recognize any of these
warning signs?
Now, the most practical part. What do
you do if you have already had even one
of those five warning episodes, even if
it felt small and vanished in under 10
minutes.
You have roughly 72 hours where a lot
can still be done to prevent a
full-blown stroke. The goal is not to
panic, but also not to waste that
window.
Stroke specialists often point out how
important it is not to be completely
alone after a suspected transient
attack. This is worth planning ahead
with your family and your doctor,
especially if you live by yourself. If
another more serious episode happens and
you suddenly cannot speak or move, you
need another person who can see it, call
emergency services, and get to you
quickly.
Many people find it helpful to tell a
close person what happened and make sure
someone can reach them easily over the
next couple of days.
That is a reasonable thing to bring up
with your health care provider.
Stroke guidelines also advise against
driving yourself after a possible TIA.
Losing vision or arm control for even a
few seconds at highway speed is
life-threatening for you and everyone
around you. It is worth talking ahead of
time with your doctor about what
transportation plan makes sense in your
situation if something like this ever
happens, so you are not tempted to just
drive yourself in.
Checking blood pressure is usually among
the first steps in almost any acute
situation. If you or someone near you
can measure it and the top number, the
systolic pressure, is around 180 or
higher and the bottom number, the
diastolic, is around 110 or higher, that
fits the picture of a hypertensive
crisis, not just elevated blood
pressure. A crisis like that is itself a
strong warning sign for stroke, and
calling emergency services right away is
what standard guidelines often
recommend. Ask your doctor explicitly
about this threshold, so you know in
advance when to treat it as an
emergency.
One rule from stroke medicine is strict.
Never start blood-thinning drugs like
aspirin, anticoagulants, or similar
medications on your own based on a
friend's advice or something you read
online. There are two main types of
stroke, ischemic where a vessel is
blocked and hemorrhagic where a vessel
is bleeding.
Thinning the blood can help in certain
ischemic situations, but in a
hemorrhagic stroke, it can make the
bleeding faster and larger which can
kill a person more quickly. The only way
to tell the difference reliably is with
brain imaging, usually a CT scan in a
hospital. No doctor can look at someone
and be 100% certain which type is
happening without a scan. So, instead of
self-treating, the right move is to get
evaluated and let a medical team decide.
While waiting for help or on the way to
care, body position matters. Lying down
is generally better than sitting bolt
upright because it helps blood flow to
the brain. Many clinicians suggest a
comfortable flat position with the legs
slightly raised above chest level to
support circulation and ease the heart's
work. The head should be neutral, not
bent sharply forward and not thrown back
so that neck vessels are not kinked. It
is also wise to avoid smoking, alcohol,
or exposure to hot baths or very hot
showers in that moment since sudden
vessel dilation in an already unstable
circulation can make things worse.
Double-check this with your own doctor.
Having a written list of all the
medications you take regularly kept
somewhere easy to find is a small step
that can save precious minutes for
emergency teams.
Something many people get wrong. If 72
hours pass and no new episode happens,
that does not mean you are in the clear.
It means you were given a second chance
and you still need to use it.
Three evaluations worth asking about.
There are three evaluations worth
requesting at your next medical visit.
The first is a carotid duplex
ultrasound, a specialized scan of your
neck arteries that shows both the
structure of the vessel and how blood is
actually moving through it. If the
artery is narrowed by more than 70%
surgeons may recommend a procedure to
physically remove the plaque and in
modern practice it is a routine surgery
that saves tens of thousands of lives
every year.
The second is the HbA1c blood test which
reflects your average blood sugar over
the past 3 months, not just a single
fasting snapshot, making it excellent at
catching pre-diabetes before it has
quietly damaged your vessels for years
without a formal diagnosis.
The third is Holter monitoring, a
24-hour heart rhythm recording that
catches dangerous rhythm problems like
atrial fibrillation, which can come and
go and be completely missed by a
standard short ECG in a clinic. If AFib
is found, well-studied anticoagulant
medications can cut stroke risk by
roughly 60 to 70%. That is not an
inevitable outcome. That is something
you and your cardiologist can actively
work on together.
Bringing it all together.
Stroke is not a lightning bolt from a
clear sky. It is a predictable event
that usually announces itself in advance
and the patients who do best are the
ones who come in prepared, who know what

E se ti dicessi che il tuo cervello
potrebbe averti già inviato un
avvertimento dell'imminente ictus e che
tu l'abbia completamente ignorato? Ogni
40 secondi, da qualche parte su questo
pianeta, qualcuno viene colpito da un
ictus. Nel tempo in cui finisci di
leggere questa frase, un altro cervello
è stato colpito. Ogni anno, l'ictus
uccide quasi 6 milioni di persone nel
mondo, è la seconda causa di morte e
il motivo principale per cui le persone
subiscono disabilità permanenti. La
parte che nessuno spiega abbastanza
chiaramente. In un gran numero di casi,
il cervello ti invia segnali molto
specifici ore o addirittura giorni
prima che si verifichi il grande ictus.
Devi solo sapere come riconoscerli.
Prima di iniziare, se non ti sei ancora
iscritto, ti consiglio di premere quel
pulsante e attivare la campanella per
non perdere mai altri consigli sulla
salute pensati apposta per te. Se ti
piace questo video, scrivi uno nei
commenti. In caso contrario, scrivi
zero per farmi sapere come posso creare
contenuti migliori per te. L'ictus non
è solo "stavi bene, sei caduto, ti sei
svegliato in ospedale". Nella maggior
parte dei casi, l'ictus è il punto di
arrivo prevedibile di vasi sanguigni
che si degradano da anni. Se qualcosa
è prevedibile, è almeno in parte
prevenibile. Questo è il senso di ciò
che sto condividendo con te oggi. Due
eventi molto diversi. Quando le persone
parlano di ictus, in realtà si
riferiscono a due eventi cerebrali
molto differenti. Uno è l'ictus
emorragico. Un vaso sanguigno nel
cervello si rompe. Il sangue si riversa
dentro o intorno al cervello, formando
un coagulo che comprime il tessuto
cerebrale, portando molti di questi
pazienti al decesso. L'altro è l'ictus
ischemico. Un vaso non si rompe, ma si
ostruisce. Il flusso sanguigno si
interrompe in una parte del cervello e
le cellule cerebrali in quella zona
iniziano a morire in circa 4-6 minuti.
Gli ictus ischemici rappresentano circa
l'85%di tutti gli ictus. Quindi è su
questo che mi concentrerò oggi. Per
capire perché ogni minuto conta, devi
avere un'idea di quanto sia esigente il
tuo cervello. Il tuo cervello pesa
circa 1,4 kg, circa il 2%del tuo peso
corporeo. Ma consuma circa il 20%
dell'ossigeno che respiri e circa il 25
%di tutto il glucosio che circola nel
tuo sangue. È un centro di controllo
che non si spegne mai e richiede un
rifornimento costante. Se tagli quel
carburante anche solo per pochi minuti,
le cellule iniziano a morire in modo
irreversibile. Ecco perché i medici
dicono che l'ictus è una corsa contro
il tempo. È letteralmente una corsa
per salvare il tessuto cerebrale prima
che vada perso per sempre. Le basi sono
state gettate anni fa. La maggior parte
delle persone non coglie ciò che sto
per dire. Perché un'arteria cerebrale
si blocchi improvvisamente, di solito
ci sono voluti anni di preparazione. Le
pareti del vaso sono state danneggiate,
materiale e coaguli si sono accumulati
e l'apertura si è ristretta sempre di
più. Non si tratta di un'esplosione
dal nulla. È l'ultimo passo di un
lungo processo. Lungo questo percorso,
il tuo corpo invia solitamente dei
segnali di avvertimento. Il problema è
che nessuno ti ha mai insegnato a
interpretarli. In medicina, questi
primi segnali di allarme sono chiamati
attacco ischemico transitorio, o TIA in
breve. Transitorio significa
semplicemente temporaneo. Va e viene.
Immagina un'arteria carotide, l'arteria
principale del collo che trasporta il
sangue dal cuore al cervello. Nel corso
degli anni, una placca grassa si forma
sulla parete interna proprio dove
l'arteria si biforca. L'apertura si
restringe lentamente. Poi, a un certo
punto, il vaso, già stretto, entra in
un breve spasmo. Il flusso sanguigno si
ferma per qualche secondo o qualche
minuto e l'area cerebrale alimentata da
quell'arteria, in pratica, si spegne
per quel breve periodo. Vedi o avverti
un sintomo di ictus. Poi lo spasmo si
rilassa, il flusso sanguigno riprende,
il sintomo svanisce e pensi di essere
di nuovo a posto. Ciò che la ricerca
dimostra è che un attacco ischemico
transitorio precede molto spesso un
ictus ischemico maggiore. Di solito
entro le successive 72 ore. Quei tre
giorni sono la tua finestra temporale
in cui il disastro può ancora essere
prevenuto. La maggior parte delle
persone non sfrutta questa finestra
perché l'episodio di avvertimento è
stato breve, strano e poi è passato.
Quindi, si convincono a non prenderlo
sul serio. Questi episodi di
avvertimento durano solitamente da
circa mezzo minuto a forse 10 minuti.
È esattamente per questo che passano
inosservati. Puoi essere in cucina,
sotto la doccia, scendere da un'auto, e
quando ti fermi a riflettere, il
sintomo è già passato. Ma ognuno di
questi episodi è il tuo cervello che
invia un messaggio finale molto chiaro.
Sto per trovarmi in gravi guai. Voglio
illustrarti i cinque grandi segnali
d'allarme e spiegare non solo come
appaiono, ma cosa sta realmente
accadendo dentro il tuo corpo ogni
volta. Segnale di avvertimento numero
uno: cecità temporanea da un occhio.
Ti alzi, cammini verso la cucina e
improvvisamente un occhio diventa scuro
o annebbiato, come se qualcuno avesse
tirato giù una tenda nera su
quell'occhio o avesse sporcato la lente
con del fango grigio. Sbatti le
palpebre un paio di volte, magari ti
stropicci l'occhio, e nel giro di pochi
secondi o un minuto al massimo, la
vista ritorna. Quindi, dai la colpa
all'esserti alzato troppo in fretta o a
troppo tempo passato davanti allo
schermo. In realtà, quella tendina è
quasi sempre un minuscolo coagulo o un
piccolo frammento di placca staccatosi
dalla parete della carotide, risalito e
che ha occluso brevemente l'arteria che
irrora l'occhio. L'arteria che porta il
sangue all'occhio non è un tubicino
isolato. È un ramo diretto della
carotide interna che nutre il cervello.
Quando il coagulo o il frammento di
placca si incastra in quella piccola
arteria oculare, il sangue non riesce a
passare. Così la retina, il tessuto
sensibile alla luce, perde il suo
apporto sanguigno per un momento e lei
vede oscurità o una macchia anziché
un'immagine nitida. Quando il coagulo
si sposta e il flusso sanguigno
riprende, la vista torna e lei si sente
fortunato. È stato fortunato perché
quello stesso coagulo avrebbe potuto
spostarsi di 2 millimetri in un'arteria
cerebrale e, invece di un oscuramento
di un minuto, si sarebbe trovato di
fronte a perdita permanente della
parola, paralisi di un braccio e una
gamba o la morte. I medici hanno un
nome classico per quell'oscuramento di
un occhio: amaurosi fugace, che
significa letteralmente cecità
passeggera. I neurologi trattano questa
espressione come un allarme antincendio
. Se un paziente descrive un episodio
simile, viene sottoposto a valutazione
urgente perché il rischio di un vero
ictus nelle ore successive è elevato.
I registri ospedalieri mostrano un
modello in cui una persona ignora due o
tre di questi episodi oculari e quello
subito successivo è quello grave al
cervello. Segnale d'allarme numero due:
improvviso intorpidimento o formicolio
su un lato. Il termine medico è
parestesia, ma può immaginarlo come se
la sua pelle fosse "ubriaca". Può
riguardare l'intero braccio, solo la
mano, metà del viso o persino un
intero lato del corpo. Si percepisce
come punture di spilli, come cotone o
come se quella parte del corpo si fosse
trasformata in gomma. Il dettaglio
chiave è che compare dal nulla mentre
è seduto, cammina o parla, dura pochi
minuti e poi scompare da solo.
Probabilmente le sarà capitato di
dormire sul braccio, causando una
compressione del nervo che provoca
intorpidimento, il quale svanisce
quando si muove. Quello è diverso. lì
. Il suo cervello e il midollo spinale
stanno bene. Ha schiacciato un nervo e
non appena il flusso sanguigno e la
posizione si normalizzano, la
sensibilità ritorna in un minuto o due
. Con un TIA, il problema non è nel
braccio. È nell'area cerebrale che
mappa la sensibilità di quel braccio,
e l'episodio non ha nulla a che fare
con la postura. Un'altra cosa che vale
la pena sapere: i sintomi dell'ictus
sono solitamente unilaterali perché
ogni emisfero cerebrale controlla e
percepisce il lato opposto del corpo.
Quando entrambe le mani si
intorpidiscono uniformemente, ciò
indica più spesso problemi alla
colonna cervicale. Ma un improvviso
intorpidimento unilaterale che svanisce
dopo pochi minuti è un valido motivo
per controllare il rischio di TIA e
ictus. Segnale d'allarme numero tre,
un'improvvisa perdita di coordinazione.
La camminata da ubriaco. Sei su una
superficie piana e familiare e, dal
nulla, il tuo piede poggia nel posto
sbagliato. La gamba sembra debole o
gommosa, barcolli contro il muro per un
secondo o vieni colto da un'improvvisa
e forte sensazione di vertigine che ti
costringe ad afferrarti a una sedia o
allo stipite della porta, anche se non
stavi girando. Non hai fatto scatti con
la testa e non ti sei appena alzato dal
letto. La parte del cervello che ti
mantiene in equilibrio e coordina i
movimenti fluidi si chiama cervelletto.
Si trova nella parte bassa e posteriore
del cranio, come un piccolo cervello
extra. Calcola costantemente dove si
trova il tuo corpo nello spazio e
quanta forza deve applicare ogni
muscolo per farti camminare dritto
invece che a zig-zag. Il cervelletto
riceve il suo apporto di sangue dalle
arterie che corrono attraverso le ossa
del collo fino alla parte posteriore
della testa. Ciò che i medici chiamano
sistema vertebrale. Se il flusso
sanguigno in quelle arterie cala
bruscamente, anche solo per pochi
secondi, il cervelletto va praticamente
in tilt. È allora che improvvisamente
devii di lato, fai un passo falso o
avverti una violenta vertigine senza un
motivo apparente. Nella pratica clinica
, ho visto persone giustificare questi
episodi con scarpe scomode, stanchezza
o pressione alta, per poi scoprire in
seguito che si trattava di attacchi
cerebellari transitori. La vertigine
benigna ha solitamente un fattore
scatenante chiaro. Girarsi nel letto,
ruotare rapidamente la testa, una nota
patologia dell'orecchio interno.
Tuttavia, una vertigine intensa e
spontanea, unita a difficoltà a
camminare dritti, va trattata come un
possibile TIA finché un medico non
esclude una causa vascolare. Segnale
d'allarme numero quattro, un linguaggio
che improvvisamente si interrompe.
Prima di proseguire, voglio chiarire
una cosa. Se ogni tanto non riesci a
ricordare il nome del tuo vicino o
dimentichi temporaneamente la parola "
spazzolino", non è un segno di ictus.
È il normale fenomeno della "parola
sulla punta della lingua", che accade
più spesso quando sei stanco o
stressato. Ciò che preoccupa i
neurologi è qualcosa di ben diverso.
Quando il tuo linguaggio si interrompe
improvvisamente in modo così grave che
persino tu senti che c'è qualcosa che
non va. Nella maggior parte delle
persone, esistono due aree principali
del linguaggio nel cervello. Entrambe
solitamente nell'emisfero sinistro.
Un'area, spesso chiamata area di Broca,
ti aiuta a formare le parole e a
inviare istruzioni chiare ai muscoli
della lingua, delle labbra e della
mascella. Quando quella regione perde
afflusso sanguigno, potresti capire
tutto ciò che dicono gli altri. Sai
cosa vuoi rispondere, ma non riesci a
pronunciare le parole. Escono
biascicate, spezzate o bloccate.
L'altra area, spesso chiamata area di
Wernicke, ti aiuta a comprendere il
linguaggio e a organizzare le tue frasi
affinché abbiano senso. Quando quella
zona è in difficoltà, una persona
può parlare in modo fluente ma dire
cose prive di senso, come un’insalata
di parole, e potrebbe non capire frasi
semplici che le vengono rivolte. Se uno
qualsiasi di questi problemi di
linguaggio si manifesta improvvisamente
e poi svanisce dopo pochi minuti, è un
classico sintomo di TIA, non è "ero
solo stanco". Non puoi ignorare un
linguaggio confuso solo perché si è
risolto da solo. È come se l'allarme
di casa tua suonasse, si fermasse da
solo e tu decidessi che probabilmente
non era nulla. Quinto segnale di
avvertimento: vitiligine combinata con
nuovi mal di testa insolitamente forti.
Il quinto segnale di avvertimento è
meno ovvio e sorprende la maggior parte
delle persone. È una combinazione di
determinati cambiamenti cutanei più
nuovi mal di testa insolitamente forti.
La condizione della pelle è la
vitiligine. Macchie di pelle pallida o
completamente bianca dove le cellule
che producono pigmento hanno smesso di
funzionare. La vitiligine è un
processo autoimmune, il che significa
che il sistema immunitario inizia ad
attaccare le tue stesse cellule
pigmentarie come se fossero estranee.
Quando il tuo sistema immunitario perde
il bersaglio in questo modo, spesso non
si ferma a un solo organo. In molte
persone, quello stesso processo
autoimmune può infiammare
silenziosamente anche il rivestimento
interno dei vasi sanguigni. Quel
rivestimento interno è chiamato
endotelio, un sottile strato
microscopico di cellule che ricopre
l'interno di ogni arteria come una
superficie antiaderente super liscia.
Quando l'endotelio è sano, i
componenti del sangue scorrono e nulla
vi aderisce davvero. Quando viene
danneggiato dall'infiammazione, diventa
ruvido e cicatrizzato e le sostanze
iniziano ad attaccarsi. Colesterolo,
piastrine e varie proteine
infiammatorie formano nel tempo i semi
di placche e coaguli. La sola
vitiligine non ti condanna a un ictus.
Ma se oltre a questo sviluppi frequenti
mal di testa insolitamente intensi che
non corrispondono al tuo schema
abituale, quella combinazione merita un
adeguato controllo vascolare piuttosto
che un approccio attendista. I mal di
testa in generale sono complicati
perché molte persone incolpano i
problemi ai vasi sanguigni quando il
vero problema è altrove. Una causa
molto comune di dolore alla testa
quotidiano o frequente è l'usura delle
piccole articolazioni tra la seconda e
la terza vertebra cervicale. In pratica
, artrite al collo. Quella
degenerazione articolare può irritare
i nervi vicini e inviare dolore alla
testa, cosa che non ha nulla a che fare
con un'arteria cerebrale bloccata.
Oltre a ciò, molte persone convivono
con un'ernia del disco cervicale non
diagnosticata. E se non la tratti mai,
nei casi gravi, può minacciare
l'apporto nervoso alle braccia o alle
gambe. I mal di testa non dovrebbero
essere semplicemente anestetizzati con
pillole a lungo termine. Devono essere
analizzati con un medico, soprattutto
quando cambiano carattere o si
presentano insieme ad altri segnali di
avvertimento come quelli appena
descritti. Cosa fare se si riconosce
uno di questi segnali di avvertimento?
Ora, la parte più pratica. Cosa fare
se si è già avuto anche solo uno di
quei cinque episodi premonitori, anche
se è sembrato lieve ed è svanito in
meno di 10 minuti? Si hanno a
disposizione circa 72 ore in cui si
può ancora fare molto per prevenire un
ictus conclamato. L'obiettivo non è
farsi prendere dal panico, ma nemmeno
sprecare questa finestra temporale. Gli
specialisti dell'ictus sottolineano
spesso quanto sia importante non
restare completamente soli dopo un
sospetto attacco transitorio. Vale la
pena pianificare in anticipo con la
famiglia e il medico, soprattutto se si
vive da soli. Se si verifica un altro
episodio più grave e all'improvviso
non si riesce a parlare o a muoversi,
serve qualcun altro che possa
accorgersene. chiamare i soccorsi e
raggiungerti rapidamente. Molte persone
trovano utile informare una persona
cara dell'accaduto e assicurarsi che
qualcuno possa raggiungerle facilmente
nei due giorni successivi. È un
argomento ragionevole da discutere con
il proprio medico curante. Le linee
guida per l'ictus sconsigliano inoltre
di guidare dopo un possibile TIA.
Perdere la vista o il controllo del
braccio anche solo per pochi secondi
mentre si è in autostrada è
pericoloso per te e per chi ti circonda
. Vale la pena parlare in anticipo con
il proprio medico di quale piano di
trasporto sia più adatto alla propria
situazione, così da non essere tentati
di mettersi alla guida. Il controllo
della pressione sanguigna è
solitamente uno dei primi passi in
quasi ogni situazione acuta. Se tu o
chi ti sta vicino potete misurarla e il
valore massimo, la pressione sistolica,
è intorno a 180 o più e il valore
minimo, la diastolica, è intorno a 110
o più, ciò rientra nel quadro di una
crisi ipertensiva, non di una semplice
pressione alta. Una crisi del genere è
di per sé un forte segnale di allarme
per l'ictus e chiamare subito i
soccorsi è ciò che le linee guida
raccomandano spesso. Chiedi
esplicitamente al tuo medico riguardo a
questa soglia, così da sapere in
anticipo quando trattarla come
un'emergenza. Una regola della medicina
per l'ictus è ferrea. Non iniziare mai
ad assumere anticoagulanti come
l'aspirina o farmaci simili di tua
iniziativa, basandoti sui consigli di
un amico o su ciò che leggi online.
Esistono due tipi principali di ictus.
Ischemico, dove un vaso è ostruito, ed
emorragico, dove un vaso sta
sanguinando. Fluidificare il sangue
può aiutare in certe situazioni
ischemiche, ma in un ictus emorragico
può rendere l'emorragia più veloce e
grave, il che può uccidere una persona
più rapidamente. L'unico modo per
distinguere in modo affidabile i due
casi è tramite l'imaging cerebrale,
solitamente una TAC in ospedale. Nessun
medico può guardare una persona ed
essere sicuro al 100%di cosa stia
accadendo senza una scansione. Quindi,
invece dell'automedicazione, la mossa
giusta è farsi valutare e lasciare
decidere al team medico. Mentre si
aspetta aiuto o ci si reca alle cure,
la posizione del corpo è importante.
Sdraiarsi è generalmente meglio che
stare seduti dritti perché favorisce
l'afflusso di sangue al cervello. Molti
medici suggeriscono una posizione
comoda e distesa, con le gambe
leggermente sollevate sopra il livello
del petto per favorire la circolazione
e alleggerire il carico del cuore. La
testa deve essere in posizione neutra,
non piegata bruscamente in avanti né
all'indietro, affinché i vasi del
collo non siano compressi. È anche
saggio evitare fumo, alcol, bagni caldi
o docce bollenti in quel momento,
poiché un'improvvisa dilatazione dei
vasi in una circolazione già instabile
può peggiorare le cose. Verifica
questo aspetto con il tuo medico di
fiducia. Avere un elenco scritto di
tutti i farmaci che assumi regolarmente
, conservato in un posto facile da
trovare, è un piccolo passo che può
far risparmiare minuti preziosi alle
squadre di emergenza. Qualcosa che
molti sbagliano. Se passano 72 ore e
non si verifica alcun nuovo episodio,
non significa che sei fuori pericolo.
Significa che ti è stata data una
seconda possibilità e devi comunque
sfruttarla. Tre valutazioni su cui vale
la pena informarsi. Ci sono tre
valutazioni che vale la pena richiedere
alla tua prossima visita medica. La
prima è l'ecocolordoppler dei vasi
sovraortici, una scansione
specialistica delle arterie del collo
che mostra sia la struttura del vaso
che il reale flusso sanguigno. Se
l'arteria è ristretta per oltre il 70%
, i chirurghi potrebbero consigliare
una procedura per rimuovere fisicamente
la placca. E nella pratica moderna, è
un intervento chirurgico di routine che
salva decine di migliaia di vite ogni
anno. La seconda è l'esame del sangue
HbA1c, che riflette la glicemia media
degli ultimi 3 mesi, non solo
un'istantanea a digiuno, rendendolo
eccellente per rilevare il pre-diabete
prima che danneggi silenziosamente i
vasi per anni senza una diagnosi
formale. La terza è l'holter cardiaco,
una registrazione del ritmo cardiaco di
24 ore che rileva pericolosi problemi
di ritmo come la fibrillazione atriale,
che può apparire e scomparire e
passare inosservata a un ECG standard
in clinica. Se viene riscontrata
fibrillazione atriale, farmaci
anticoagulanti ben studiati possono
ridurre il rischio di ictus di circa il
60-70%. Non è un risultato inevitabile
. È qualcosa su cui tu e il tuo
cardiologo potete lavorare attivamente
insieme. Tiriamo le somme. L'ictus non
è un fulmine a ciel sereno. È un
evento prevedibile che solitamente si
annuncia in anticipo. E i pazienti che
ottengono i risultati migliori sono
quelli che arrivano preparati, che
sanno quali domande porre e che non
ignorano i piccoli segnali di
avvertimento. Se riconosci uno dei
cinque segnali di avvertimento nella
tua vita, anche se risale a mesi fa,
scrivilo in modo semplice e porta la
lista al tuo medico. Non affidarti alla
memoria. Chiedi direttamente se
dovresti sottoporti a controlli per
attacchi ischemici transitori e se
un'ecografia carotidea, l'emoglobina
glicata o l'Holter siano appropriati
per il tuo caso. Tutto ciò che è
stato trattato qui ha scopo puramente
informativo ed educativo; usarlo come
punto di partenza per un confronto
reale con il tuo medico sarà sempre
più utile che provare a gestire le
cose da solo. Se questo video ti è
piaciuto, lascia un commento scrivendo
uno. In caso contrario, sentiti libero
di commentare con zero. Il tuo feedback
per noi è molto importante. Non
dimenticare di mettere mi piace,
condividere e iscriverti al nostro
canale YouTube per altri contenuti come
questo. Grazie per aver guardato, e
brindiamo a vivere la vita alle tue
condizioni.

What if I told you that the blurry
vision stealing your independence isn't
old age? It's silent damage happening
while you sleep and a few ordinary
fruits eaten before bed could start
reversing it tonight.
Most people over 60 just accept it. The
dry, scratchy eyes every morning,
squinting at the menu,
headlights at night that leave you
gripping the steering wheel tighter than
you used to. They think it's just part
of getting older.
But here's what most doctors don't take
the time to explain. It's not always
just age. The American Optometric
Association warns that once you're past
60, your eyes become far more vulnerable
to dry eyes, cataracts, macular
degeneration, and sudden vision changes.
And the National Eye Institute confirms
that vision loss among Americans is
rising faster than ever before.
What makes this especially dangerous is
when the damage happens. At night, while
you think your body is resting, your
retina doesn't always get the oxygen it
needs. The delicate cells responsible
for clear vision begin breaking down
slowly and silently. Most people don't
notice until the damage is already done.
So, the question I hear almost every
week in my office is this. Why is my
vision blurry? And is there a natural
way to fix it without expensive drugs or
risky surgery?
Here's the hard truth. Eye drops,
stronger glasses, even surgery, they
treat the symptoms. They don't touch the
root cause. That's exactly why the
vision care industry makes billions
every year while older adults keep
losing ground. A 2023 study in JAMA
Ophthalmology confirmed that age-related
retinal damage begins with silent
oxidative stress and inflammation. Most
active at night when your eyes should be
healing.
But here's the good news. Recent
research has found that certain everyday
fruits contain powerful compounds your
eyes crave during sleep. Nutrients that

Japan leads the world in healthy aging — and it's not by accident. In this video, you'll discover five traditional Japanese-inspired movements that have helped generations of older adults maintain powerful, stable legs well into their 80s and beyond. Unlike generic workout routines, these exercises target the specific muscles, reflexes, and coordination patterns that actually prevent falls and protect independence — including the toe grip reflex most seniors have never trained, and the ankle mobility that quietly determines how safely you clear the ground with every step. No equipment needed. Just five simple movements you can start today, right at home.

¿Qué tal si te dijera que el secreto
para llegar a los 80 o 90 años con
confianza no es un suplemento, una
dieta especial ni nada que encuentres
en una farmacia, sino una serie de
pequeños movimientos diarios que toda
una cultura practica en silencio desde
hace generaciones? Camina por casi
cualquier barrio en Japón y verás
algo que desafía discretamente lo que
la mayor parte del mundo cree sobre el
envejecimiento. Personas de 70 y 80
años subiendo escaleras sin dudar,
levantándose del suelo sin usar las
manos y caminando con pasos firmes y
seguros. Esto no es suerte y tampoco es
simplemente genética. Japón tiene una
de las mayores concentraciones de
personas que superan los 100 años en
todo el mundo. Y lo que más destaca
para quienes estudian el envejecimiento
saludable no es solo cuánto viven,
sino lo móviles que se mantienen
mientras lo hacen. Mientras tanto, en
gran parte del mundo occidental, la
fuerza de las piernas comienza a
disminuir notablemente después de los
50. Y ese declive está estrechamente
ligado a una caminata más lenta, falta
de equilibrio y caídas, una de las
mayores amenazas para la independencia
en la vejez. Aquí está la parte
alentadora. Si las personas mayores en
Japón pueden mantener piernas fuertes
y capaces hasta una edad avanzada, eso
nos dice algo importante. No es algo
inalcanzable. Es un método, un
conjunto de pequeños movimientos
repetidos integrados en la vida
cotidiana. Hoy, voy a enseñarte cinco
de esos movimientos. Cada uno inspirado
en prácticas japonesas tradicionales
para lograr piernas fuertes y estables.
Y cada uno puedes hacerlo en casa a
partir de hoy. Antes de comenzar, si
aún no te has suscrito, te recomiendo
encarecidamente que presiones el botón
de suscripción ahora mismo y actives
la campana de notificaciones. De esa
manera, nunca te perderás otro consejo
de salud hecho especialmente para ti.
Si disfrutas este video y te resulta

si sientes que podría mejorar o cubrir

Leo cada comentario y realmente uso sus

funcionan estos movimientos? Lo que

mientras estás sentado, marchar en el

diferente de las piernas y el sistema

vivir en Japón, ni necesitas equipo

Ejercicio uno, levantarse del suelo.
Sentarse y levantarse al estilo Seiza.
En los hogares japoneses, sentarse
directamente en el piso, en un cojín,
un taburete bajo o simplemente con las
piernas cruzadas, ha sido común por
generaciones, incluso mientras los
hogares occidentales cambiaban casi
totalmente a sillas y sofás. Lo que
parece una simple diferencia de estilo
de vida es en realidad una prueba de
fuerza diaria que la mayoría de los
adultos mayores occidentales ya no
reciben. bajarte por completo al piso y
volver a levantarte sin apoyarte en las
manos. Piensa en la frecuencia con la
que un día típico en un hogar sin
sillas exige este movimiento. Sentarse
a comer, levantarse para abrir la
puerta, acomodarse en un cojín para
hablar con la familia. Cada repetición
, sin que nadie la llame ejercicio,
refuerza silenciosamente la misma
fuerza profunda en caderas y rodillas
que determina si un adulto mayor
occidental puede levantarse del suelo
sin ayuda después de un tropiezo o si
necesita auxilio para hacerlo. Empieza
cerca de un sofá o silla resistente
por seguridad. De pie, baja para
sentarte en un cojín o en el piso,

gradualmente cuánto te apoyas en tus

directamente en transiciones más

caminata de deslizamiento surashi. Este

una especie de equilibrio controlado
con centro de gravedad bajo que es
directamente útil para mantenerse
firme en la vida diaria. Lo que
diferencia esto de caminar normalmente
es el contacto constante con el suelo.
Debido a que el pie nunca se separa del
suelo, tu sistema nervioso debe seguir

ajustándose en tiempo real conforme
cambia tu peso. Es un desafío de
equilibrio mucho más exigente de lo

un pie hacia adelante por el suelo sin

para alcanzar al otro. Continúa este

movimiento lento y deliberado, ya que

Nunca en calcetines, sobre madera o

solo unos pocos pasos por la
habitación y aumenta la distancia

text:
Frequent tripping after 70 is not always caused by carelessness. Weak muscles at the front of the shins and hips can reduce foot clearance, shorten your stride, and make rugs, thresholds, or uneven sidewalks more dangerous. In this senior health video, you will learn five simple, equipment-free exercises that help strengthen the muscles responsible for lifting your toes and driving your legs forward. Practiced consistently, these movements may improve walking control, balance, confidence, and everyday mobility. Always use a sturdy support, move slowly, and speak with your healthcare professional if you recently had surgery, significant pain, or dizziness.

subtitles.plaintext:
What if the next time you trip, your
body cannot catch itself fast enough?
You are walking across the kitchen
carrying coffee when your toe catches
the edge of a rug. In one split second,
a step can become a dangerous fall.
Most people assume tripping is bad luck,
clumsiness, or simply part of getting
older. But repeated trips are often a
warning that two muscle groups have
weakened. These muscles should lift your
toes and drive your leg forward, keeping
your foot safely above the ground with
every step.
The good news is that you can train
them. Today, I will show you five
exercises designed to strengthen both
muscle groups, retrain your foot-lifting
pattern, and help you clear everyday
obstacles more safely. You can practice
them at home without equipment.
You will learn why your foot keeps
catching the floor and how to correct
the problem before a stumble becomes a
fall.
Before we dive in, if you haven't
subscribed yet, I recommend you hit that
button and turn on the bell, so you
never miss another health tip made just
for you. If you enjoy this video, type
one in the comments. If not, type zero
to let me know how I can make better
content for you.
Why do adults over 70 trip more often?
Every step requires your foot to swing
forward and clear the ground, and two
muscle groups must activate at the right
time.
The first group is the ankle
dorsiflexors along the front of your
shin. They lift your toes in the front
of your foot as your leg swings. When
they weaken, your toes may drag and
catch a rug, threshold, or sidewalk.
The second group is your hip flexors at
the front of the hip. They drive your
knee forward and help lift the leg. When
they become weak, your foot stays closer
to the floor, forcing the ankle muscles
to compensate.
Imagine opening a door with a stiff
hinge. It moves, but not far enough. The
same thing happens when these muscles
lose strength. Your foot does not rise
high enough. Fortunately, both groups
can become stronger with consistent
exercise.
Exercise one, the stair activation.
Why it matters.
This is the foundation of everything.
The single most direct exercise you can
do to target both muscle groups
responsible for tripping at the exact
same time.
Most exercises work one muscle group at
a time. The step lift is different. It
combines an ankle movement and a hip
movement into one fluid two-stage
repetition, which means every single rep
you complete is training the precise
sequence of muscle activations that your
body needs to execute with every step
you take.
What makes this exercise so powerful for
seniors over 70 is not just what it
strengthens, it is what it retrains.
After months or years of shuffling
dragging steps, the neural pathway that
tells your ankle to lift and your hip to
drive has grown faint from disuse.
The step lift sends a clear strong
signal along that exact pathway with
every repetition. Over time, the signal
gets stronger, the muscles respond
faster, and your foot begins to clear
the ground the way it was always
designed to.
How to do it.
All you need is the bottom step of your
staircase or a low sturdy footstool.
Stand tall near the wall or handrail
with one hand available for support at
all times. Place the foot of your
working leg on the step, heel resting on
the step, toes pointing upward. Your
standing leg should be slightly bent,
never locked. Back straight, chin level,
shoulders relaxed.
Now, lift your toes as high as you
possibly can toward your shin, keeping
your heel firmly on the step. Hold for 1
second. Feel the front of your shin
engage. Then, while keeping those toes
lifted, slowly raise your knee upward
toward your chest as high as you
comfortably can.
Hold for 1 second at the top, then lower
your knee slowly, lower your toes, and
return to the starting position. That is
one complete repetition.
Do 10 repetitions on each leg. Complete
two sets per session. Rest 30 seconds
between sets.
What to focus on?
After several repetitions, you should
feel a mild fatigue building along the
front of your shin and at the front of
your hip. That is exactly right. That is
the signal that these muscles are being
challenged and will grow stronger. Do
not rush the lowering phase. The
controlled descent builds the eccentric
strength your muscles need to stabilize
your foot when it lands on the ground
with each real step.
Progress tip.
Once 10 repetitions feel manageable,
increase to 12, then 15 over the
following weeks. The goal is steady
progressive challenge, not speed, not
strain. Slow and controlled always wins.
If you're still watching and finding
these insights helpful, please comment
number one below to let me know you're
with me.
Now, let's move on to point number two.
Exercise two, the shin power walk.
Why it matters.
The step lift builds the strength. The
toe raise walk teaches your body to use
that strength while actually moving,
which is when it matters most. There is
a critical difference between being able
to lift your toes while standing still
and being able to lift them
automatically, repeatedly, and with full
control while your body is in motion.
This exercise bridges that gap. It
trains your ankle dorsiflexors to fire
consistently with every step, building
the habit of proper foot clearance into
your actual walking pattern rather than
just into a stationary exercise.
Many seniors over 70 who trip regularly
have no difficulty lifting their toes
when they are standing still and paying
full attention.
The problem occurs when they are
walking, thinking about something else,
carrying something, or simply moving
through their day on autopilot.
The toe raise walk trains the reflex to
fire automatically without conscious
thought, which is exactly what you need
it to do in a real tripping situation.
How to do it?
Find a clear hallway or open space along
a wall. Stand at one end with one hand
lightly touching the wall for support if
needed.
Begin walking, but with each step before
your foot swings forward, consciously
lift your toes upward as high as you can
and keep them lifted throughout the
entire swing phase until your heel makes
contact with the ground. Heel touches
down first, toes still lifted, then the
rest of the foot follows. Take 10 steps
forward this way, turn carefully using
small controlled steps, and walk back 10
steps. That is one set. Complete three
sets with a 30-second rest between each
one.
What to focus on?
Keep your gaze forward, not down at your
feet. In real life, your ankle needs to
lift automatically while your eyes are
focused on where you are going, not on
the mechanics of your own feet. This
exercise begins building that automatic
quality from the very first step. If you
feel unsteady, slow down and keep your
hand on the wall. Speed is never the
goal here.
Progress tip.
Once this feels natural and automatic on
flat ground, try the same walk on a
slightly different surface, from
hardwood to carpet, for example.
The slight variation in texture and
resistance forces your nervous system to
adapt and generalize the pattern, which
is precisely what you need for
real-world safety, where surfaces are
rarely perfectly uniform.
Exercise three, the hip drive march.
Why it matters.
If the ankle dorsiflexors are one half
of the tripping equation, the hip
flexors are the other, and this exercise
targets them directly. When your hip
flexors are strong, they generate the
forward drive that lifts your entire
thigh with each step. That thigh lift is
what creates the chain reaction. Thigh
rises, knee comes up, ankle clears the
ground. When the hip flexors are weak,
that chain reaction breaks down at the
very first link, and no amount of ankle
strength can fully compensate for a hip
that is not doing its share of the work.
The high knee march rebuilds this
lifting reflex from the ground up. It is
simple, it requires no equipment, and it
directly mimics the hip movement your
body needs with every single walking
step. Done consistently, it restores the
power and speed of that hip drive, which
means your foot spends more time safely
in the air and less time dangerously
close to the ground where tripping
happens.
How to do it.
Stand behind a sturdy chair with both
hands resting lightly on the back for
support. Stand tall, back straight, chin
level, shoulders relaxed. Slowly lift
your right knee upward towards your
chest as high as you comfortably can
without leaning your upper body
backward. Hold for two full seconds at
the top, then lower your foot back to
the floor slowly and with complete
control.
Repeat on the left side.
That is one full repetition. Complete 15
repetitions on each side, 30 total lifts
at a slow, deliberate pace throughout.
What to focus on.
The lifting work should come entirely
from your hip, not from momentum, not
from leaning back, not from a quick
swing of the leg. Slow, intentional,
powerful. And the lowering phase matters
just as much as the lift. Do not let
your foot drop. Control the descent all
the way to the floor. This eccentric
control is what stabilizes your foot the
moment it returns to the ground in real
walking. And it is one of the most
under-trained qualities in seniors over
70
Progress tip.
As this becomes easier, practice the
march while moving slowly forward
through your hallway. Lifting each knee
deliberately before stepping, then
placing your heel down first. You're now
combining this exercise directly with
the toe raise walk from exercise two,
creating the closest possible simulation

Et si la prochaine fois que vous
trébuchez, votre corps ne parvenait
pas à se rattraper assez vite ? Vous
traversez la cuisine avec votre café,
quand votre orteil accroche le bord
d'un tapis. En une fraction de seconde,
un simple pas peut devenir une chute
dangereuse. La plupart des gens pensent
que trébucher est dû à la malchance,
à la maladresse, ou simplement au
vieillissement. Mais les trébuchements
répétés sont souvent le signe que
deux groupes musculaires se sont
affaiblis. Ces muscles doivent relever
vos orteils et avancer votre jambe,
gardant votre pied en sécurité
au-dessus du sol à chaque pas. La
bonne nouvelle, c'est que vous pouvez
les entraîner. Aujourd'hui, je vais
vous montrer cinq exercices conçus
pour renforcer ces deux groupes
musculaires, rééduquer votre façon
de lever le pied et vous aider à
franchir les obstacles du quotidien
plus sûrement. Vous pouvez les
pratiquer à la maison sans aucun
équipement. Vous apprendrez pourquoi
votre pied accroche le sol et comment
corriger le problème avant qu'un faux
pas ne devienne une chute. Avant de
commencer, si vous n'êtes pas encore
abonné, je vous recommande de cliquer
sur le bouton et d'activer la cloche
pour ne plus manquer aucun conseil
santé fait pour vous. Si vous aimez
cette vidéo, tapez un dans les
commentaires. Sinon, tapez zéro pour
me dire comment je peux améliorer mon
contenu pour vous. Pourquoi les adultes
de plus de 70 ans trébuchent-ils plus
souvent ? Chaque pas exige que votre
pied avance et qu'il dégage le sol. Et
deux groupes musculaires doivent
s'activer au bon moment. Le premier
groupe est constitué des muscles
dorsifléchisseurs de la cheville, le
long de votre tibia. Ils soulèvent vos
orteils et l'avant de votre pied
pendant que votre jambe oscille. Quand
ils faiblissent, vos orteils peuvent
traîner et accrocher un tapis, un
seuil ou un trottoir. Le second groupe
est celui des fléchisseurs de la
hanche, à l'avant de la hanche. Ils
propulsent votre genou vers l'avant et
aident à soulever la jambe. Quand ils
deviennent faibles, votre pied reste
plus près du sol, forçant les muscles
de la cheville à compenser. Imaginez
que vous ouvriez une porte avec une
charnière rigide. Elle bouge, mais pas
assez loin. La même chose se produit
lorsque ces muscles perdent de leur
force. Votre pied ne monte pas assez
haut. Heureusement, les deux groupes
peuvent être renforcés grâce à des
exercices réguliers. Premier exercice
: l'activation sur marche. Pourquoi
est-ce important ? C'est la base de
tout. C'est l'exercice le plus direct
pour cibler simultanément les deux
groupes musculaires responsables des
trébuchements. La plupart des
exercices travaillent un groupe
musculaire à la fois. Le "step lift"
est différent. Il combine un mouvement
de cheville et de hanche en une
répétition fluide en deux étapes, ce
qui signifie que chaque répétition
entraîne la séquence précise
d'activations musculaires dont votre
corps a besoin à chaque pas. Ce qui
rend cet exercice si efficace pour les
seniors de plus de 70 ans, ce n'est pas
seulement ce qu'il renforce. C'est ce
qu'il rééduque. Après des mois ou
des années à marcher en traînant les
pieds, la voie nerveuse qui commande à
votre cheville de se lever et à votre
hanche de propulser s'est affaiblie par
manque d'usage. Le « steplift »
envoie un signal clair et puissant le
long de ce chemin précis à chaque
répétition. Avec le temps, le signal
devient plus fort. Les muscles
réagissent plus vite et votre pied
commence à bien décoller du sol,
comme il a toujours été conçu pour
le faire. Comment le faire ? Tout ce
dont vous avez besoin, c'est de la
première marche de votre escalier ou
d'un marchepied bas et solide.
Tenez-vous droit près d'un mur ou
d'une rampe, avec une main disponible
pour vous soutenir à tout moment.
Placez le pied de la jambe que vous
travaillez sur la marche, le talon
posé sur celle-ci, les orteils
pointés vers le haut. Votre jambe
d'appui doit être légèrement
fléchie, jamais verrouillée. Le dos
droit, le menton à l'horizontale, les
épaules détendues. Maintenant, levez
vos orteils aussi haut que possible
vers votre tibia, en gardant fermement
le talon sur la marche. Maintenez
pendant une seconde. Sentez l'avant de
votre tibia se contracter. Ensuite,
tout en gardant les orteils relevés,
montez lentement votre genou vers votre
poitrine, aussi haut que vous le pouvez
confortablement. Maintenez pendant une
seconde en haut. Puis abaissez votre
genou lentement. Abaissez vos orteils
et revenez à la position de départ.
Ceci constitue une répétition
complète. Faites 10 répétitions pour
chaque jambe. Réalisez deux séries
par séance. Reposez-vous 30 secondes
entre les séries. Sur quoi se
concentrer ? Après plusieurs
répétitions, vous devriez ressentir
une légère fatigue s'installer le
long de l'avant du tibia et au niveau
de l'avant de la hanche. C'est
exactement ce qu'il faut. C'est le
signal que ces muscles sont sollicités
et qu'ils vont se renforcer. Ne
précipitez pas la phase de descente.
La descente contrôlée développe la
force excentrique dont vos muscles ont
besoin pour stabiliser votre pied
lorsqu'il se pose au sol à chaque vrai
pas. Conseil de progression. Une fois
que 10 répétitions semblent gérables
, passez à 12, puis à 15 au cours des
semaines suivantes. L'objectif est un
défi progressif et constant, pas de la
vitesse, ni de la tension excessive. La
lenteur et le contrôle gagnent
toujours. Si vous regardez toujours et

point numéro deux, deuxième exercice,
la marche avec renforcement des tibias.
Pourquoi est-ce important ? Le «
steplift » renforce la puissance. La
marche avec relèvement des orteils
apprend à votre corps à utiliser
cette force en mouvement, ce qui est le
moment où cela compte le plus. Il
existe une différence cruciale entre
être capable de lever les orteils en
restant immobile et être capable de le
faire automatiquement, de manière
répétée et avec un contrôle total
pendant que votre corps est en
mouvement. Cet exercice comble ce
fossé. Il entraîne vos muscles
fléchisseurs dorsaux de la cheville à
se contracter systématiquement à
chaque pas, intégrant l'habitude d'un
bon dégagement du pied dans votre
marche réelle plutôt que dans un
simple exercice statique. De nombreuses
personnes de plus de 70 ans qui
trébuchent régulièrement n'ont
aucune difficulté à lever les orteils
lorsqu'elles sont immobiles et qu'elles
y prêtent attention. Le problème
survient lorsqu'elles marchent, pensent
à autre chose, portent un objet ou se
déplacent simplement en pilote
automatique. Le lever d'orteils
entraîne le réflexe de contraction
automatique sans réflexion consciente,
ce qui est exactement ce dont vous avez
besoin en situation réelle de
trébuchement. Comment le réaliser ?
Trouvez un couloir dégagé ou un
espace ouvert le long d'un mur.
Tenez-vous à une extrémité, une main
effleurant le mur pour vous soutenir si
nécessaire. Commencez à marcher, mais
à chaque pas, avant que votre pied ne
parte vers l'avant, levez consciemment
les orteils le plus haut possible et
maintenez-les levés tout au long de la
phase de balancement jusqu'à ce que
votre talon touche le sol. Le talon
touche le sol en premier, les orteils
toujours levés, puis le reste du pied
suit. Faites 10 pas vers l'avant de
cette façon. Tournez prudemment en
faisant de petits pas contrôlés et
revenez sur 10 pas. C'est une série.
Effectuez trois séries avec 30
secondes de repos entre chacune. Sur
quoi se concentrer ? Gardez le regard
vers l'avant, pas sur vos pieds. Dans
la vie réelle, votre cheville doit se
lever automatiquement pendant que vos
yeux sont fixés sur votre destination,
et non sur la mécanique de vos pieds.
Cet exercice commence à construire
cette qualité automatique dès le
premier pas. Si vous vous sentez
instable, ralentissez et gardez la main
sur le mur. La vitesse n'est jamais
l'objectif ici. Conseil de progression.
Une fois que cela devient naturel et
automatique sur sol plat, essayez la
même marche sur une surface
légèrement différente, du parquet
vers un tapis, par exemple. La légère
variation de texture et de résistance
force votre système nerveux à
s'adapter et à généraliser le
schéma, ce qui est précisément ce
dont vous avez besoin pour la
sécurité réelle où les surfaces
sont rarement uniformes. Troisième
exercice, la marche avec impulsion de
la hanche. Pourquoi est-ce important ?
Si les fléchisseurs dorsaux de la
cheville constituent la moitié de
l'équation du trébuchement, les
fléchisseurs de la hanche en sont
l'autre moitié, et cet exercice les
cible directement. Lorsque vos
fléchisseurs de hanche sont forts, ils
génèrent l'impulsion vers l'avant qui
soulève toute votre cuisse à chaque
pas. C'est ce soulèvement de la cuisse
qui crée la réaction en chaîne. La
cuisse monte, le genou s'élève, et la
cheville dégage le sol. Lorsque les
fléchisseurs de la hanche sont faibles
, cette réaction en chaîne se brise
dès le premier maillon. Et aucune
force de cheville ne peut entièrement
compenser une hanche qui ne fait pas sa
part du travail. La marche avec montée
de genoux reconstruit ce réflexe de
levage à partir de zéro. C'est simple
. Cela ne nécessite aucun équipement
et reproduit directement le mouvement
de hanche dont votre corps a besoin à
chaque pas de marche. Pratiqué
régulièrement, cela restaure la
puissance et la vitesse de cette
poussée de hanche, ce qui signifie que
votre pied passe plus de temps en
sécurité dans les airs et moins de
temps dangereusement près du sol, là
où les trébuchements surviennent.
Comment faire. Tenez-vous derrière une
chaise robuste avec les deux mains
posées légèrement sur le dossier
pour vous soutenir. Tenez-vous droit,
dos redressé, menton parallèle au sol
, épaules détendues. Levez lentement
votre genou droit vers votre poitrine
aussi haut que vous le pouvez
confortablement sans pencher le haut du
corps en arrière. Maintenez la
position pendant deux secondes
complètes en haut. Ensuite, reposez
votre pied sur le sol lentement et avec
un contrôle total. Répétez sur le
côté gauche. Cela constitue une
répétition complète. Effectuez 15
répétitions de chaque côté, soit 30
montées au total à un rythme lent et
délibéré tout au long. Sur quoi se
concentrer ? L'effort de levage doit
venir entièrement de votre hanche, pas
de l'élan, pas en vous penchant en
arrière, ni d'un balancement rapide de
la jambe. Lent, intentionnel, puissant,
et la phase de descente compte tout
autant que la montée. Ne laissez pas
votre pied retomber. Contrôlez la
descente jusqu'au sol. Ce contrôle
excentrique est ce qui stabilise votre
pied au moment où il touche le sol
lors de la marche réelle et c'est
l'une des qualités les moins
travaillées chez les seniors de plus
de 70 ans. Conseil de progression.
Lorsque cela devient plus facile,
pratiquez la marche en avançant
lentement dans votre couloir, en levant
chaque genou délibérément avant de
faire un pas, puis en posant le talon
en premier. Vous combinez maintenant
cet exercice directement avec la marche
sur talons de l'exercice 2, créant la
simulation la plus proche possible
d'une mécanique de marche sûre et
correcte que vous pouvez entraîner
chez vous. Si vous regardez toujours et

text:
Poor leg circulation is one of the most common — and most ignored — health concerns for adults over 70. When blood flow slows down in the legs, it can lead to swelling, cramping, numbness, fatigue, and even serious complications like blood clots. The good news? Simple, targeted movements done daily can naturally stimulate blood flow, activate key muscle groups, and help your legs feel lighter and stronger. In this video, you'll learn easy exercises you can do in bed, in a chair, or standing — no equipment needed. Start today and feel the difference in as little as 30 seconds.

destinés à soutenir votre santé, pas
à la mettre en danger. Voici quelques
règles simples que je veux que vous
suiviez chaque fois que vous faites
cette routine. Premièrement, ne forcez
jamais si vous ressentez une douleur
vive. Il y a une différence entre la
brûlure saine des muscles qui
travaillent et la douleur vive et
soudaine d'un problème potentiel. Si
quelque chose vous fait mal d'une
manière qui ne semble pas normale,
arrêtez immédiatement. Reposez-vous
et si la douleur persiste, contactez
votre professionnel de santé.
Deuxièmement, commencez doucement,
surtout pendant la première semaine.
Votre corps a besoin de temps pour
s'adapter. Même si ces mouvements
semblent faciles le premier jour,
donnez à vos muscles, vos
articulations et votre système
circulatoire le temps de réagir. En
faire trop trop tôt est l'une des
erreurs les plus courantes, et cela
mène à des courbatures et au
découragement qui poussent les gens à
abandonner avant même de voir des
résultats. Troisièmement, soyez
régulier. La plus grande différence
entre ceux qui voient une réelle
amélioration de leur circulation
sanguine et ceux qui n'en voient pas ne
réside pas dans l'intensité de
l'effort, mais dans la régularité.
Même 5 à 10 minutes par jour,
effectuées systématiquement,
donneront de bien meilleurs résultats
qu'une séance intense une fois par
semaine. Voyez cela comme une habitude
quotidienne, au même titre que se
brosser les dents, et non comme une
solution miracle unique. Quatrièmement
, hydratez-vous bien. Boire
suffisamment d'eau tout au long de la
journée joue un rôle majeur dans la
circulation et le fonctionnement
musculaire. Si vous êtes déshydraté,
votre sang s'épaissit légèrement et
devient plus difficile à pomper
efficacement dans votre corps.
L'habitude simple de boire de l'eau
régulièrement tout au long de la
journée peut réellement soutenir tout
ce que vous faites avec ces exercices.
Et enfin, soyez patient avec vous-même
. Le changement ne se produit pas
toujours du jour au lendemain, mais il
finit par arriver. Beaucoup de gens
sentent leurs jambes plus légères,
moins gonflées et plus énergiques en
seulement quelques jours après avoir
commencé une telle routine. Pour
d'autres, cela prend quelques semaines.
